The coupon for each period is C x n/N x day -count- fraction, where C is the fixed coupon (e.g. 10%), n is number of days 10y CMT fixing is in the range of (0, K), N is total number of business days in the period (e.g. 63 days), day -count-fraction is the period length annualized. With the strike K set well above the forwards, the digital floorlets are usually deep ITM at inception. Since the probability of being below or above K sums up to 1, it gives the parity equation: digital floorlet(K) + digital caplet(K) = 1. So a short digital floorlet equals a long digital caplet minus a fixed unit cashflow. In other words, the dealer: • pays the full coupon (e.g. 10%) unconditionally; and • owns a strip of OTM digital caplets at high strike K which pays when fixing is higher than K. Each digital caplet can be replicated by a tight payer spread – long a payer at K and short a payer at K plus epsilon. The dealer is long that spread and as we see below in Figure 3, vega goes from positive below the strike (as it needs volatility to be ITM ) to 0 at the strike (as it doesn’t need extra volatility to stay ITM ) to negative above the strike (as it reduces the probability of ITM as volatility goes up). Consequently, dealers must hedge unfavorably due to the notes’ negative convexity profile ; i.e. as 10y CMT rates rise and vol/skew firms up, dealers need to buy more ATM vol/payer skew to hedge the increasingly larger negative vega (see Figure 3). Mechanically, a key factor here is that 10y CPI expectations have been below 5y for the entirety of the post-COVID period, a flip from the pre-COVID norm. In any case, in a world with declining medium-term inflation expectations, it is no wonder that 5y5y CPI swaps have not returned to the "old normal" levels. FIGURE 2. Compounding these pressures, we and the market expect growth to slow into 2027. Fiscal arithmetic can differ from political calculus. High real rates raise the government’s interest bill, while slower growth weakens revenues and worsens the denominator of the debt-to-GDP ratio. If fiscal uncertainty pushes risk premia higher, the BRL weakens and inflation expectations rise, leaving the BCB with limited room to ease even as activity slows. Fiscal policy, monetary policy and currency moves can then reinforce one another. From a market perspective, however, immediate fiscal balance is often not required. A clear, credible plan that convinces investors debt will eventually stabilize is often sufficient. The complication is that reforms that would most clearly change the trajectory—slower growth in mandatory expenditures, reduced indexation and greater budget flexibility—are also among the most politically challenging. A center-right Congress might find a path to such reforms, but building a durable coalition seems difficult. records.text: Euro Area Watch | 13 October 2026 5 Rates Edvard Davidsson MLI (UK) edvard.davidsson@bofa.com BTPs: attractive enough? BTPs initially proved resilient during the recent sell-off but were eventually pulled wider by weakness in OATs. Since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, 10y BTP-Bund spreads have largely traded as a beta to energy prices and rates, although the relationship has recently weakened as the French sell-off became the dominant driver (Exhibit 5). Relative cheapness should attract some foreign private demand. Domestic investors however appear to have limited capacity to add bonds to portfolios but, following some diversification, could come back to BTPs if levels are attractive enough. The front end should remain better supported by retail demand and subdued issuance if rates stay elevated, with a potential S&P upgrade providing an additional tailwind. By contrast, the long end faces a more challenging supply-demand backdrop, given limited scope to reduce issuance further and the risk of slowing inflows to Italian lifers. records.text: Marija Veitmane Anthi Tsouvali 15 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Week 1 of 3Q26 Earnings : Good Headlines, Messy Details The earnings season is off to a mixed start. Headline beats remain encouraging, but the details are more nuanced: bank earnings are losing momentum, IT demand remains remarkably resilient, while the global consumer continues to weaken. In short, earnings are holding up, but the underlying dispersion is widening. 1. Banks earnings are slowing after blow-out 2Q quarter with non-interest income declining (Figure 2). Indeed, we flagged this risk in the past as non -interest income tends to be volatile which could be problematic when valuations and positioning are stretched. This perhaps explains recent position unwind in the sector (Figure 3). We are particularly concerned about European banks, where holdings remain extended while lending demand is slowing faster than in the US. 2. Strong guidance in the IT sector. So far, we heard earnings reports from ASML and TSMC – both beat expectations and reported no signs of demand slowing. If anything, capacity constraints, rather than softer demand, remain the main brake on earnings growth. It is worth noting that earnings expectations are already exceptionally high, at roughly three times the market average, but continue to rise (Figure 4). Microsoft’s infrastructure strategy is designed to maximize flexibility across a broad set of enterprise workloads, rather than optimize for the needs of frontier model development. Capex decisions are driven by customer demand visible today, and a change in frontier model pacing does not alter those demand signals. While Microsoft could direct incremental capacity toward frontier workloads, the priority remains infrastructure that can serve a broad cohort of customers across many workloads. The decision to step back from portions of Stargate capacity and all of 4Q’s $51bn RPO increase coming from non frontier customers support this view. Microsoft also has several years of data observing how its most sophisticated AI customers have scaled, providing greater visibility into how enterprise AI demand may evolve over the next three to five years. We believe the ROIC debate matters more than the capex debate. Earlier in the AI cycle, investor focus centered around whether demand would justify the elevated capex levels. Today, Azure remains supply constrained, Copilot monetization is improving, and M365 Commercial Cloud is expected to accelerate. records.text: M Idea 2 Too Early to Call the All-Clear We can feel the change in the weather here in Europe as temperatures begin to cool into heating season. European gas storages look modestly healthier than expected a month ago, but the picture has changed little - Europe will still enter winter with record- low pre-winter storage levels and a reduced buffer against colder weather. We now forecast inventories in our European perimeter to enter winter at 74% full, up from our previous estimate of 71%. Our two base case assumptions of 1) mild winter weather and 2) a recovery in Middle East Gulf LNG flows by Q1 27 had started to materialize in September. Qatar has been exporting LNG at their highest level since the conflict began (~30% pre-conflict levels), and weather across Europe has been very mild, with temperatures running 7% above the seasonal norm over the last six weeks. This weighed on European gas prices in late September, easing some of the bullish sentiment that had built across the market. However, our bullish gas market thesis remains predominantly a winter story, and the heating season is only just beginning. In our last note, we highlighted "we see the upside as predominantly winter-driven, with fewer fundamental catalysts through September and October". Profit-taking as TTF approached €80/MWh in early September was therefore unsurprising, given the looser balances expected over these months. records.text: M Idea 2 Details How will the rise in US rates affect Asia? In our recent discussions with investors, one of the frequently asked questions is how the rise in US rates will affect Asia. One investor recalled that whenever US rates moved up as much as they have recently, it has tended to create stress for EM economies. (For our EM macro strategists' latest views, please see Global EM Strategy: What Now For EM? (29 Sep 2026)). With the recent intra-day high of 5.36%, the US10Y bond yield is at its highest level since 2002. With the bond markets still pricing in three more rate hikes by the Fed over the next 12 months, some investors are raising concerns about the implications for Asia. At the outset, we believe this cycle is different and that Asia as a region is better positioned than previous cycles. The nature of the cycle matters – while the US cycle resembles the 1990s…: When you think about past rate hike cycles, the one that is the most similar to the US right now was in the 1990s. Back then, as is the case now, there was a backdrop of strong tech and overall non-residential (property) capex. The US economy is in a technology-led capex cycle, just like it was in the 1990s. In the 1990s, the rapid adoption of personal computers drove a sustained increase in IT investment, and now AI is catalysing technology investment. In the 1990s, the Fed hiked rates but productivity growth continued to accelerate as a result of the tech adoption. The expansion cycle was sustained, but

Fading monetary debasement vs growing fiscal debasement – The fear of Fed losing political independence was the most important driver of the January gold rally, leading to a collapse in US$ and all-time high gold prices. Market concerns on monetary debasement faded as the Fed has been hawkish on inflation since Warsh took over, and the debasement trade recently shifted to fiscal problems. However, fiscal debasement has a less straightforward impact on gold. While gold demand should theoretically benefit from debasement hedging, higher government bond yields (still considered risk-free practically) lead to higher opportunity costs of holding gold, a zero-couple non-yielding asset. As rates rise though, the US government may be more and more tempted to debase fiscally by buying bonds. Gold vs other precious metals – We sense a lot less market interest on silver and PGMs than last year as the price outperformance against gold reversed and as market fundamentals turn quiet (on PGMs)/bearish (on silver substitution/thrifting). We stick to our longstanding view that silver and platinum will continue to track gold in direction with high beta, while palladium will continue to lag given its negative long-term fundamental outlook. Swedish inflation surprises to the downside, Swiss CPI hits 1% Swedish headline inflation (CPIF) accelerated sharply to 1.5% y/y in September. Key Takeaways Traditional models apply one elasticity across every country, even though trade's sensitivity to FX moves varies widely. We instead built country-specific models to isolate how much — and how reliably — FX can do the rebalancing work on its own. To that end, we ran a counterfactual exercise: what if the exchange rate were the only lever available to close a country's external gap, with every other channel held fixed? In that world, our results suggest a CNY move of +22%, JPY of +20% and USD 12% depreciation could be required to bring external balance. In practice, FX alone can't rebalance an economy, but investors want to know what role it could play so a reference scale is useful to understand how much burden falls on other savings and investment policies. Trade volumes do not respond to an exchange-rate move at once. Contracts are priced in advance, buyers take time to switch suppliers, and producers take time to add capacity. An error-correction model captures this by estimating two quantities separately: the long-run elasticity, which is how far volumes move once adjustment is complete, and the speed of adjustment (φ), which is the share of any deviation from that long-run relationship closed each quarter. We use the conditional ARDL form of Pesaran, Shin and Smith (2001), which recovers the long-run relationship without first classifying each series as trend- or difference-stationary, a classification that is rarely clean in quarterly trade data. records.text: nted annually with €10bn from the infrastructure fund: The special fund "Climate and Transformation" (KTF) was set up in 2010 to financially support the energy transition. The KTF receives income from the national CO2 price. From 2025 onward, it obtains €10bn annually from the infrastructure special fund (over 10 years totalling €100bn). Spending continues to focus on energy cost subsidies: The total investment-related spending of the KTF is broadly unchanged in 2027 at €22.9bn compared to 2026 at €22.2bn. Much of the work in IMF and policy circles continues to emphasize the saving and investment decisions that generate current accounts (see here) while BIS research highlights the increasingly important role of financial flows, investment income and valuation effects in determining how those imbalances accumulate and ultimately adjust (see here). Our work adds a complementary, market-relevant question to that debate: how much of the rebalancing could exchange rates themselves actually deliver by affecting trade volumes? To do this, we adopt a differentiated approach relative to traditional models, including a country-by-country analysis of export and import responses, while also weighting the components of each country's trade basket by currency-invoicing use rather than the currency of the trade partner. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Nickel 1) Will Indonesian policy continue to be restrictive on domestic production? Indonesia dominates global nickel production and growth. The country cut mining quotas (RKABs) by one-third for 2026, or 15% below 2025 actual production, with only limited additional quota released so far. The market awaits the release of 2027 quotas where further discipline could bring support to nickel prices, although signs of flexibility or a more generous quota system could ease market tightness fears. 2) How are high sulphur prices impacting production and cost curves? HPAL (High- Pressure Acid Leaching) has driven 36% of Indonesia's production growth since 2020 and accounts for 16% of total output. However, with 10t of sulphur per tonne of nickel, it has faced both supply and cost challenges since the Middle East conflict. Indonesia's sulphur imports are down 13% YTD. while the sulphur price has risen from ~$500/ in January to > $1,000/t, adding ~$5,000/t to costs. With annual contract negotiations coming up, we may see some delays to new HPAL capacity, keeping 2027 tighter. Indonesia is also facing water shortages due to El Niño, driving production cuts at IMIP. 3) Will nickel find a higher floor? records.text: Tight spreads and flat curves leave little cushion against another rates shock A further challenge for the spread/rates correlation this year has been the tight starting level of spreads, leaving limited room for additional spread compression to offset a move higher in government yields. Even after the recent widening, spreads remain tight relative to their post-2010 history across much of the IG and HY markets (Exhibit 6). Credit spread curves also offer limited additional compensation for extending maturity. The 2s10s credit spread curves remain relatively flat in both USD and EUR IG and have been resilient to both steepening and flattening in government bond curves in recent years (Exhibit 7). As a result, investors receive relatively little incremental spread compensation for extending either credit or duration risk, leaving unhedged portfolios more vulnerable to another rates-led risk-off. records.text: ab 12 October 2026 Global Research Global Strategy US Consumer Credit Outlook: Resilient Aggregate, Weaker Middle Executive summary The US consumer remains resilient in aggregate, supported by moderate leverage and higher asset values, even as debt-service burdens rise. Resilience is uneven: middle- income households are near historical averages but weaker relative to history than other cohorts, making the middle, rather than only the lower-income tail, the key group to watch. What is new: the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances shows aggregate consumer health is the second strongest since 1995, despite broadly rising payment burdens and concentrated stress in cards, autos and weaker borrowers. Debt and spending remain concentrated among stronger households, while mortgages—the dominant liability— remain the principal buffer against broader stress. Outlook: We expect further credit normalization without a broad consumption downturn. Spending remains concentrated among stronger households; a labor-market shock that broadens stress into the middle is the principal risk. Market implications: US HY consumer cyclicals trade 27 bp through the index, near their historical median. Better post-COVID quality limits contagion, but softer consumer indicators argue against chasing the rally; we see 10–15 bp of relative downside vs. the index. records.text: Euro Area Watch | 13 October 2026 3 National recovery plan: final stretch, but no fiscal cliff in 2027 In September 2026, Italy formally submitted its request for the tenth and final payment, worth €28.4bn. The request marks the completion of the implementation phase of Italy's €194.4bn Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP). To unlock the final tranche, Italy reported the achievement of 156 milestones and targets, bringing the total number of completed RRP objectives to 576. Given the sheer size of the final tranche, expectations in Rome are that the European Commission's assessment could take longer than previous reviews, with the actual disbursement potentially extending beyond the end of 2026. Implementation has progressed further, but official data remain scarce. As of February 2026, actual spending had reached €113.3bn, up from €104.6bn at end-2025, equivalent to around 58% of the total RRP envelope (Exhibit 2). At the same time, government administrations estimated that approximately €24.2bn of planned expenditure, largely related to infrastructure projects, will be shifted beyond the 2026 deadline. In practice, this means that fiscal support from EU funds is likely to continue even after the formal completion of the RRP. Equally important, the risk of a fiscal cliff over our forecast horizon appears limited amid the deployment of other EU funds. Large imbalances can persist for years. Currency revaluations are often in focus as markets think about how to rebalance current accounts. In theory, real appreciation makes a surplus economy's exports dearer abroad and its imports cheaper at home, shrinking the surplus as volumes adjust; a depreciation does the reverse for a deficit economy. The scale of an imbalance adjustment is governed by the price elasticity of trade...and other domestic drivers of production. Here, we focus primarily on the trade-driven imbalance and currency as the key variable; we measure a theoretical currency adjustment that could rectify any given imbalance. Such an exercise helps provide boundaries of currency movement that our FX Strategists can use to think about valuation. The current-account gap tells us whether an external position is stronger or weaker than the level justified by medium-term fundamentals. With multiple sources of potential stress still present and little evidence of a favorable catalyst on the horizon, we continue to view the risk-reward profile as unattractive and maintain our negative stance on the factor. Stay Neutral on Yield (Dividends + Buybacks): The prospect of interest rates remaining elevated for an extended period continues to limit the appeal of traditional income-oriented equities, particularly as higher risk-free yields provide investors with an increasingly competitive alternative. However, along with being under-owned, Yield also shares some characteristics with Value as an effective "anti-AI" style factor. Its exposure is concentrated in sectors such as Banks, Insurance, Oil & Gas, and Software & IT Services, leaving it relatively underrepresented in the market's dominant AI trade. As a result, any broadening of market leadership or signs of fatigue in the AI theme could provide a meaningful tailwind for the factor. While the macro backdrop remains challenging, these potential style-rotation benefits argue against an outright negative stance. On balance, the positive and negative forces appear broadly offsetting, leading us to maintain a neutral view on Yield. 13 October 2026 14 Barclays | U.S. Equity Factor Insights - October 2026

Microsoft disclosed that Maia 200 delivers up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for AI capabilities across Teams, Copilot, and Cowork vs. leading GPU infrastructure. Operating these workloads at scale directly informed the design of Maia 300. Maia 300 represents the next step in improving the cost curve. Maia 300 is n purpose built for long context reasoning, latency sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained multistep agentic workloads. Microsoft expects the system to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt vs. leading GPU based systems and up to 7x the rack scale token throughput of Maia 200 in a full 96 accelerator configuration. Software compatibility and performance have yet to be proven at production n scale - but even the Software roadmap should be further along. Our industry feedback this year suggests that Microsoft still has more work to do on its supporting Maia software stack. Microsoft’s strategy is less about building the industry’s best individual chip and more about optimizing silicon, software, networking, and datacenter infrastructure around its own workloads. Our understanding is that by definition, an ASIC is customized to a specific software roadmap, such that progress on MAI (Microsoft’s AI roadmap) also informs progress on Maia (Microsoft’s chip roadmap). 15 October 2026 8 Goldman Sachs Microsoft Corp. Rising funding costs and growing scrutiny of AI-related spending increase the likelihood that performance broadens toward more cyclical and under-owned segments of the market from the crowded AI trade. • Large-over-Small Size: Higher interest rates remain a significant headwind for smaller companies given their greater dependence on external financing. With the Russell 2000 and S&P 600 down 7.6% since the end of 1H26, versus a 4.0% gain for the S&P 500, the market continues to reward stronger balance sheets and more durable earnings profiles. • Momentum: Recent performance has been driven largely by strength in Semiconductors, AI- related beneficiaries, and energy-linked stocks, leaving the factor well positioned if those trends persist. As mentioned earlier, using the US as an example, the answer should be no and we feel the same about the euro area. In Quantitative tightening need not be frightening, we argued that unlike QE, where the signalling channel is dominant, QT's primary implications are higher net bond supply and reserve drain (money market implications). As we explain below, a halt in balance sheet reduction would reduce the net supply to the private market but we are sceptical the relief from such a measure would be permanent. After all, net supply changes do not influence the medium-term direction and level of bond yields - the macro cycle does -hence, the flow-effect is weak. Having said this, an argument can be made that pausing QT could prevent further term- premium decompression from the run-off of monetary policy portfolios when global factors are already pushing euro area term-premium higher. For example, Schnabel (2025) showed that as of October 2025, 10-year sovereign bond yields in the euro area were estimated to be still some 60bp below the level that would have prevailed in the absence of QE, ie, the stock-effect of existing holdings is still suppressing term-premium although there has been a steady decompression since QT began. In our last European Gas Manual, we discussed in detail the EU's plan to phase out the remaining Russian LNG imports into Europe in Jan 2027: Russia Gas Phaseout. Various estimates from energy consultants expect Yamal flows in Q1 2027 to be only 50-75% of Q1 2026 levels. This would imply a 1.3-2.6 Mt cut to the 5.1 Mt of Q1 27 Yamal exports. The additional tanker capacity needed to service the 78-day round trip from Yamal to China via the Cape, vs the 20-day Yamal to Western Europe roundtrip, is one of the major bottlenecks to Yamal continuing to operate at over 100% of nameplate capacity this winter. Sending Russian LNG to Asia would require Arctic ice-class vessels (Arc7) to carry volumes from the Yamal facility to the Murmansk STS zone where they are then transhipped onto a conventional LNG carrier which completes the long journey to Asia. Argus data indicates that Novatek has sufficient ice-class vessels to facilitate continual flows between Yamal and Murmansk, albeit are currently short on conventional LNG shipping capacity to support the re-routing of the majority of Yamal volumes from Murmansk to Asia. Woodmac data suggests that maintaining 100% of normal flows to Asia would require Novatek to charter ~40-45 additional conventional LNG carriers. Azure growth remains a function of both new capacity coming online and Microsoft’s allocation decisions between internal initiatives and external customers. In our view, Azure acceleration through FY27 could be achievable, not just from the puts and takes to capacity coming online, but also due to Improvements in utilization, software optimization, infrastructure efficiency, and monetization. Though concerns that the Autumn Budget would herald a shift away from fiscal prudence have dissipated, some risk premium persists, as seen in our UK political risk index (Figure 1). We attribute this to a combination of global fiscal headwinds and the idiosyncratic risks associated with a new government's first fiscal event. The budget on 28 October will prove benign overall, we expect, prioritising near-term policy stability and reducing headroom to GBP17.9bn from GBP23.6bn in March. We have maintained a fairly constructive outlook on both the UK economy and UK assets, and think this budget could provide further support, on the margin. However, as the budget is likely to stop short of addressing structural spending challenges (e.g. defence, ageing costs, and debt interest), some fiscal risk premium is likely to linger. Overall, cross-asset implied volatility remains low, with the VIX at 15 and FX volatility similarly anchored. Credit implied volatility has picked up but remains low relative to history. Within equities, unusually high dispersion has kept index-level volatility contained, with implied correlations close to historical lows across all regions. This reflects not only low correlations among stocks within the same sectors, but also very low correlations across sectors in the index (Exhibit 19). As a result, equity upside hedges into year-end are inexpensive, particularly in rate-sensitive areas of the market. By contrast, rates volatility has risen sharply alongside the bond sell-off over the summer, pushing the MOVE-to-VIX ratio to its highest level since 2024 (Exhibit 20). As discussed above, further sharp increases in rates are likely to weigh more on equities; tactically, we would sell payers on back-end rates to fund equity puts. VIX call spreads look attractive as broad downside hedges into year-end, with max-payoff ratios high relative to history (Exhibit 21). records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy A helping hand A wobble in risk assets lent a helping hand to EUR rates this week, with OATs also benefiting. ECB speak suggested limited appetite to deploy bond market tools which corroborates our view that a pause to ECB QT is unlikely. We also revisit the great HQLA rotation in bank liquidity buffers. From whatever it takes to until something breaks... This week had a bit of everything: ECB speakers from the sidelines of the IMF conference calling for further policy tightening while dismissing the need to deploy bond-market tools, a hot US CPI print, followed by a broader risk- off move and flight-to-quality. As yields have surged over the past three months, "what breaks?" has been a recurring question, and a source of hope that the bond market sell-off might stall, or better still, reverse. Zooming out of the day to day dynamics from this week, we remain broadly directionless in EUR rates and caught in cross-currents. The Gulf conflict continues to put pressure on energy prices, with the TTF Dec-26 contract now at year-to-date highs following a c.25% rally this month. The tightening in financing conditions from the broader rates sell-off may dampen the urgency for the ECB to act, allowing it to maintain its measured quarterly pace. In this energy shock, growth has been surprisingly resilient, and we get another temperature check on this with October flash PMIs next week. A downside surprise would fuel the narrative that growth is finally cracking

This analysis brings the labor market into the framework we used to assess the output gap, and which found that it explains very little of core inflation (see Mexico monetary policy: Mind the (inflation) gap, dated 20 May). Here, we look at how employment, hours and participation respond to the cycle, estimate how low unemployment can go before it puts pressure on inflation, test whether any measure of slack moves inflation, and use microdata from the national employment survey (ENOE) to measure who will be most affected by the shorter working week. Adjusting through hours and participation: Mexico has no national unemployment insurance, so few workers can afford to remain unemployed for long. In a downturn, the adjustment comes mostly through shorter hours and through people leaving the labor force. A one-point fall in the output gap raises the unemployment rate by about 0.1pp, but causes a close-to-0.8pp rise in the share of underemployed workers . The unemployment rate on its own is therefore a narrow gauge of slack . Low unemployment reflects lower equilibrium rate: Our estimate of the NAIRU, the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, fell from roughly 5% over 2008 –15 to around 2.6% in Q2 2026, in two steps . For example, Australia, Canada, Indonesia and Turkey lean toward manufactured consumer goods and capital equipment, purchases that can be deferred, reduced or substituted with domestic supply when relative prices move. • Import response is smaller where the marginal import is a necessity or an input. Japan imports almost all of its energy and a large share of its food, so a weaker yen raises the cost of the import bill without reducing the quantity. The terms of trade, not volumes, become the margin of adjustment. Korea, Thailand and the Philippines import components that are assembled and re-exported, so their import volumes follow the export cycle rather than the currency. • Part of the apparent weakness in the import response reflects how the import price is measured. The quarter that achieves this maximum statistic becomes the estimated break date. This procedure helps identify why the Asian crisis economies’ export elasticities were distorted. It filters out the level shifts during the 1998 currency crisis that were making Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines read as outliers. Once the step is in, their export elasticities move back into the range the rest of the sample occupies: in Korea and Malaysia because the speed of adjustment recovers while the exchange- rate coefficient barely moves, and in Indonesia and the Philippines because the exchange-rate coefficient itself is corrected. Southeast Asian economies (Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines) which attracted a lot of foreign capital ran a combined current account deficit of 5.5% of GDP in 1Q96. Moreover, a large number of economies were running pegged exchange rates and dependent on dollar debt for their funding, which then culminated in the Asian financial crisis. Strong exports and capex-driven cycle: As in the 2000s, Asia is benefiting from strong export growth, supported this time by the technology investment cycle in the US, which is increasing demand for the region’s electronics, capital goods and related supply-chain inputs. This external boost is being reinforced by a broader capex super-cycle within Asia, driven by rising investment in AI, energy, defence and industrial capacity. The current account surplus for the region in aggregate has risen to US$1.6 trillion (4.2% of GDP). However, unlike in the run-up to the Asian financial crisis in the 1990s, the region has not experienced a comparable buildup in leverage. Asia is therefore entering the current Fed tightening cycle with solid export and investment momentum, but without the same degree of balance-sheet issues that characterised the late 1990s. 2 Insights About State Street PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of the prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. The interactive Country Inflation Series charts overlay against the relevant official measures of inflation, in all cases non-seasonally adjusted. records.text: rice trend. What the analysis shows The framework is designed to identify the direction, breadth and momentum of pricing and inventory changes. Average price movements indicate whether pricing is firming or weakening; breadth measures show how widely that movement is distributed across products; and the company and category heatmaps identify areas of relative strength or weakness. Comparing pricing with inventory can provide an additional signal: rising prices alongside falling inventory may suggest tightening availability, while declining prices alongside rising inventory may indicate softer demand or excess supply. Interpretation and limitations The results should be treated as market indicators rather than revenue-weighted semiconductor ASP trends. Equal weighting can allow small- or low-value products to influence the average as much as high-volume products. Distributor listings may not represent realised transaction prices and may reflect currency movements, minimum-order quantities, promotions, stale listings or changes in product mix. Coverage also varies materially across companies and categories; movements based on small product counts can be volatile and disproportionately affected by individual products. Inventory values should likewise be interpreted cautiously. They represent observed distributor inventory valued at listed prices, rather than companies' total channel or balance sheet inventory. The RMB, meanwhile, is managed: its recent strength has come from the trade surplus and exporters' FX conversion, and our economists see meaningful appreciation as not the preferred adjustment channel, since without stronger domestic demand it would mainly squeeze exporters, profits and employment and reinforce deflation. In the United States, the current-account deficit is wider than its EBA norm, implying around 12% required depreciation, and the model splits cleanly on where that adjustment could come from. The export response is among the strongest in the sample, so a weaker dollar would do real work on US exports. The import response is not as strong, because US imports are currently driven by what the economy is building rather than by what foreign goods cost. The AI capex cycle is the reason: AI-linked imports have grown to close to a fifth of all US imports, and alongside strong capital-goods demand they pushed the goods deficit to a record in August. This is a J-curve on capacity rather than contracts — the servers, chips and machinery have to be imported before domestic production, productivity or service exports can respond, so the deficit widens first and improves only later. records.text: arguably stronger than crude, LNG freight rates remain depressed, in sharp contrast to the record charter rates currently being paid for VLCCs. This reflects a wave of newbuild LNG carriers ordered in anticipation of the next wave of liquefaction capacity, with vessel deliveries running ahead of LNG supply additions. The market was already oversupplied in 2024/25, and fleet growth has continued through 2026. Argus estimates a further 59 carriers will be delivered between September 2026 and March 2027, suggesting limited scope for a sustained recovery in freight rates near-term. Consequently, some of these freight costs may be considered sunk, reducing the opportunity cost of sending a cargo to Asia. For traders holding vessels under multiyear time charters, much of the freight cost is already committed, reducing the incremental cost of longer-haul deliveries to Asia. Indeed, some traders may be willing to send USGC cargoes to Asia even at inferior headline netbacks to Europe, given the risk that vessels returning sooner from shorter European voyages would remain idle in an oversupplied shipping market. This dynamic could support longer-haul LNG flows to Asia, despite the apparent netback disadvantage. Consequently, we suspect NW European LNG prices may need to trade at a sustained premium to JKM, as observed in Q1 25 and Q1 26 (Exhibit 17), to maximise LNG flows into Europe. records.text: ut the EBA CA norm allows for a substantially larger deficit of 2.3% of GDP. Relative to fundamentals, India's external position is therefore 1.6pp stronger than required, suggesting INR REER would need to appreciate 8% to bring external balance. Against zero, however, India is still running a deficit, so the direction flips to roughly 4% downward required adjustment. CHF, ILS and CLP also switch direction, while MXN moves from modest required appreciation relative to its EBA norm to essentially no adjustment against a zero balance. This contrast in the results is precisely why we choose to use the EBA CA norm as the headline benchmark: The EBA CA norm asks how far the observed current account sits from a position justified by medium-term fundamentals and desirable policies. The zero anchor instead asks what would happen if the currency had to eliminate the entire current-account surplus or deficit, irrespective of whether that external position is structurally appropriate. Therefore, the latter is useful more as a stress test or thought experiment, as it answers a different question. This wedge between the two anchors tells us how much of an economy's observed external position is structural rather than excessive. The larger the wedge, the less informative it is to interpret the headline current-account balance itself as a measure of FX adjustment pressure. Slower growth of labor input also argues for a more moderate path of potential output than the one behind Banxico’s estimate, which would make the gap less negative than the Governing Board assumes . Reform adds a risk for 2027: The transition to a 40-hour week will concentrate its effect on formal services, the segment where inflation persistence is highest. Taken together, our results suggest that the convergence of core inflation towards the 3% target is likely to be slower than the Governing Board expects, and that the balance of risks for inflation next year leans to the upside. For households, the latest BoJ Opinion Survey on the General Public's Views and Behavior showed that more than half of respondents continued to expect prices five years ahead to “go up significantly.” Including those expecting prices to “go up slightly,” 86.5% expected higher prices (Exhibit 3-Exhibit 4). The results were largely unchanged from the previous survey, although the average quantitative expectation for prices five years ahead edged down from an annualized 10.8% in 2Q26 to 10.1% (Exhibit 5). For firms, the September Tankan showed that the rise in inflation expectations paused after two consecutive quarterly increases. Lower input prices likely contributed. However, inflation expectations remained above 2% across a wide range of industries and firm sizes (Exhibit 6; see our 1 October report). Risks remain to the upside Although inflation expectations held at around 2% in 3Q26, risks remain tilted to the upside. When the BoJ conducted its Opinion Survey in August, cost pressures had yet to feed through materially to consumer prices, while various subsidies were also keeping CPI inflation below 2%. Most respondents base their expectations for future prices on recent inflation. The reacceleration in CPI inflation since September is therefore likely to push household inflation expectations higher. In particular, widespread price hikes for frequently purchased food items could push inflation expectations higher from the next survey onward (see our 2 October report)

M Global Foundation 6 The Role of FX In Reaching External Balance: A Refinement of our FEER Model James Lord, Nimish Prabhune We released our Fundamental Equilibrium Exchange Rate (FEER) model in September last year. The conversations we've had since suggested an alternative perspective on the role of FX in external adjustment, which we explore here. Our FEER model attempts to find the level of the real effective exchange rate (REER) that is consistent with external balance in the economy. In the original formulation of our model, we regressed the REER on the current account balance and a set of macroeconomic fundamentals (terms of trade, fiscal balance, net foreign assets and relative productivity) within an ARDL architecture, before substituting the IMF's EBA current account norm for the actual balance and then solving for the REER. The output is a benchmark: where the currency should sit if the external position were at the level fundamentals justify? The causal logic assumes that changes in the external position and fundamentals of the economy drive the currency, and that the currency responds to those changes. For example, a stronger current account can be associated with a stronger equilibrium currency if both are being driven by a common improvement in fundamentals, such that the stronger currency account is sustainable. It’s important to understand the baseline heading into this Budget. While the DMO/OBR’s illustrative projections from April (see Annex D) show the gross financing requirement trending lower to £211.6bn by FY30/31, this is highly unlikely to be realised. Firstly, since that update, this year’s issuance has already added a cumulative £52.5bn to the funding need over FY27 /28 to FY30/31 (this will be added on 28 October). Secondly, if we simulate for the impact of future issuance on redemptions, we can add another £83bn. This alone implies a gross financing requirement in FY30/31 closer to £285bn. If we then assume the DMO takes on the BoE’s QT sales (to be confirmed) that likely adds another £13bn or so (assuming yields unchanged) to the financing need and £300bn looks even harder to escape - Figure 9. In this context, it is worth remembering that the drop in the funding need this year was likely a blip. For FY27 /28, we suspect the gilt remit will be around £300bn (after accounting for a likely pick-up in contribution from Treasury bills to say £15bn). Guardrails and Epistemics The required-adjustment calculation is conceptually simple, but that simplicity also creates an important source of sensitivity: The current account gap enters linearly in the numerator, while the trade elasticity enters in the denominator. The mapping from CA gap to required REER move is a reciprocal, so estimation error does not pass through linearly, it passes through convexly, and the convexity is severe exactly where the parameter is small. As ηTB approaches zero, the required currency adjustment rises rapidly: Small revisions to an already-small elasticity can generate very large changes in estimated REER adjustment. records.text: Favor carry and neutral duration Overall, we think the spread/rates correlation is more likely to settle closer to zero than return quickly to a meaningfully negative regime. The sharp rise in global yields was partly driven by technical factors that exacerbated rates volatility, particularly pockets of negative convexity in Treasury futures and mortgages, according to our rates team. As these technicals become a diminishing source of further upside pressure on yields, the correlation should become less positive in the USD market. However, elevated oil prices and lingering fiscal uncertainty in Europe are likely to prevent a rapid return to a more supportive regime in both the USD and EUR market. Beyond the macro backdrop, the key signpost for credit is whether the supportive demand technical from all-in yield investors can remain intact. A sustained decline in rates volatility would improve confidence in carry-oriented strategies and reinforce the technical support that has kept spreads anchored. Conversely, persistently elevated volatility would make investors less willing to add duration-sensitive credit exposure. Reflecting this balance of risks, we favor carry with controlled duration exposure. Within credit, we retain a modest preference for USD over EUR, favor BBBs over AAs and As, and see better value in the belly of the spread curve than at the long end. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 35 Constructing the Bilateral FX Adjustment Matrix We use BIS's broad trade weights to perform this translation. For each currency, we retain the published weights on the other currencies in our model universe. The residual represents trade with currencies outside our sample, which we treat as a single rest-of- world (RoW) bucket and assume that, on average, it's anchored at fair value. This treatment of the RoW is important as it preserves the actual structure of each currency's effective basket rather than pretending that our sample represents its entire trading universe. It also gives the system a natural anchor, allowing us to recover a unique set of currency levels without imposing an additional arbitrary normalization or fitting the REER adjustments through a least-squares exercise. The resulting bilateral grid reproduces the original multilateral gaps exactly and, by construction, satisfies both symmetry and transitivity. Composition explains much of why the import side is weaker. A second reason is that, for most economies, the trade-weighted real exchange rate is not the price importers actually pay. Dominant Currency Paradigm: Actual Price Paid for Imports Standard trade theory assumes producer-currency pricing: an exporter sets its price in its own currency, so a bilateral exchange-rate move passes into the buyer’s price one for one. On that assumption the trade-weighted real exchange rate is the correct rate of what an importer faces, because it averages exactly those bilateral moves across partners. Gopinath et al. (2020) show that this is not how most trade is priced. Using customs-level bilateral price and quantity data, they find that the majority of world trade is invoiced in a third currency, one belonging to neither the exporter nor the importer, and that this currency is almost always the dollar. Their central finding is that once invoicing is accounted for, the bilateral exchange rate between trading partners has very little explanatory power for import prices. records.text: M Global Foundation 34 Converting REER to Bilateral FX Adjustments James Lord, Nimish Prabhune The analysis so far tells us how far each currency’s REER would need to move for its current account to converge to the EBA norm. But the REER is inherently a multilateral construct: it measures a currency against a trade-weighted basket rather than against any single counterpart. For clients, the more natural question is if these multilateral REER adjustments are the right starting point, what set of bilateral FX adjustments would be consistent with them? We address this through a simple thought experiment that translates the REER adjustment into a complete matrix of implied cross-currency adjustments. We would like to note that this does not introduce a new fundamental valuation signal but is more of a thought experiment that reorganizes the information already contained in the REER adjustments into the bilateral space in which FX is actually traded. From a REER adjustment to a bilateral grid The intuition rests on two basic consistency conditions. First, bilateral adjustments must be symmetric in direction: if currency A has a required upward adjustment against currency B, then B must have the equivalent required downward adjustment against A. Second, the grid must be transitive. The implied adjustment between A and C should be the same whether we compare them directly or move through currency B; otherwise the resulting matrix would contain internally inconsistent triangular rela

Historically, our composite energy index weighted oil and TTF equally, reflecting similar direct HICP contributions via similar shares of household consumption expenditure. Stronger oil pass-through and weaker gas pass-through largely offset, leaving overall headline sensitivity broadly unchanged. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 9 Our model results indicate that the trade channel can help narrow current-account gaps, but its strength is modest and uneven, and it varies with each economy's trade structure. Export volumes respond more strongly to the real exchange rate than import volumes, so a greater share of any FX-driven adjustment comes through exports. Exports are also the better-measured half of the model: most export elasticities are statistically significant, while import elasticities are estimated with less precision. We draw the following key conclusions: • Export volumes respond most where goods compete on price at the margin. Thailand and China show some of the largest responses in the sample. Their manufacturers face close regional substitutes, so relative prices move market share. Mexico is the clearest case in Latin America, with an export base integrated into US manufacturing supply chains. Its response is well identified, but compressed by the 50–60% imported content of its autos and IT hardware: a weaker peso raises input costs alongside export revenue. • Export volumes respond least where the domestic currency does not set the price foreign buyers pay. For example, Brazil and Norway export oil, iron ore and other commodities priced in dollars on world markets. The economic size of the effect is negligible: Even in the trough of the pandemic, with an output gap close to −12%, slack subtracted at most around 0.2pp from services inflation on a four-quarter average, and its effect on core inflation was smaller still. When the labor market was tight, in 2018–19 and again in 2023, it added less than 0.1pp. In the current cycle its contribution is effectively zero (see Figure 8). A short sample and noisy quarterly data limit the precision of these estimates, so the absence of a detectable effect is partly a statement about the evidence. However, we think that the estimates are small enough that a negative gap of plausible size could not deliver meaningful disinflation. records.text: Global Gas and Power Insights 12 October 2026 Citi Research 3 The reversal in gas flows between Ukraine and CEE not only eases CEE gas markets, but it also reduces the region’s call on gas from NW European (NWE), thereby alleviating concerns over low NWE inventories, particularly in Germany. Ukraine’s net imports from CEE totaled close to 6.5 bcm in 2025 and averaged ~0.7 bcm/m during the Nov’25-Mar’26 winter. Simply eliminating these imports would improve the CEE balance by 0.7 bcm/m relative to last winter. Moreover, Ukraine became a net exporter to CEE in September 2026, supplying 0.1 bcm, and could re- export as much as 1 bcm to Europe during the coming winter (Montel, Sept 3 2026; Semafor, Sept 10 2026). Importantly, we would expect this constraint to remain issuer- and structure-specific rather than represent a broad closure of AI financing markets. Aggregate AI Capex will Survive, The Marginal AI Project May Not For the AI financing cycle, we think the first constraint from higher rates will be on the marginal cost of capital rather than its aggregate availability. Stated differently, if yields remain near current levels, capital may still be available, but not at a price that every marginal project can support. The impact will first be felt further down the quality spectrum, with leveraged Datacenter Operators more vulnerable than higher-quality Hyperscalers. We would therefore expect the initial adjustment to a higher-for-longer all-in yield regime to come through greater project selectivity and changes in financing mix rather than an immediate reduction in AI capex. Projects requiring substantial incremental funding before reaching cash generation should face a disproportionately higher hurdle rate, while borrowers with stronger contractual support, limited remaining funding needs or greater structural protection should prove more resilient. records.text: The Factors Behind the Rise in US Yields 10y Treasury yields have risen by over 100bp since the start of the year and 130bp since the year-to-date lows set on the eve of the US-Iran conflict. Front-end and nearer-term forwards have driven a larger portion of the point-to-point move since the end of February, but forwards further out the curve were responsible for the most recent phase of the selloff (Exhibit 1). Despite the ongoing focus on inflation risks, breakevens have played a limited role through the broader reset, with higher longer-term yields disproportionately driven by the real component. From a global standpoint, the selloff since late August has come in two phases. The first, which spanned Jackson Hole and the September central bank decisions, featured bearish impulses from all major markets. The second, which covers the last three weeks, has been almost exclusively US-driven within core rates markets, with Germany in particular turning into an exporter of bullish shocks onto global duration amid greater stress in sovereign spreads (Exhibit 2). records.text: M Global Foundation 24 Computing the Required FX Adjustment James Lord, Nimish Prabhune The required FX adjustment framework reduces the rebalancing question to two inputs: First, how far the current account sits from its benchmark (CAgap) Second, how sensitive that the current account balance is to the exchange rate ηTB We measure the first using both the IMF EBA norm and, as a deliberately more mechanical cross-check, a zero current account anchor. For the second, we leverage the country- specific export and import elasticities estimated in the preceding The MS Trade Elasticity Model: Long-run, Economy-Specific and Price Aware section to derive each economy’s trade-balance sensitivity to the REER. The required REER adjustment is then the ratio of CAgap and absolute value of ηTB as shown in Exhibit 21 . Exhibit 21: CA Gap to REER Adjustment translation Source: Morgan Stanley Research Defining the Gap How far is the actual C/A balance from the sustainable level? For each economy, we measure the current account as the trailing four-quarter sum of the balance divided by the trailing four-quarter sum of nominal GDP to remove seasonality from the series. The primary measure of external imbalance is the distance of this actual current account balance from the IMF EBA CA norm as shown below in Exhibit 22 . M Global Foundation 28 South Korea is another intuitive example: Its underlying current-account surplus of 13.1% of GDP sits 9.8pp above its 3.3% EBA norm. Combined with an estimated trade-balance semi-elasticity of -0.19, the raw calculation implies an appreciation slightly in excess of our upper bound, leaving KRW at the +50% cap. Hungary also has a sizeable positive external gap, while China combines a 3.2pp surplus relative to its norm with a -0.15 elasticity to produce around 22% required upward adjustment. Conversely, economies whose current account positions are well below their EBA CA benchmarks tend to show room for depreciation, which would encourage competitiveness and an improved CA position. Romania's underlying deficit is 5.7pp of GDP weaker than its norm, while Turkey's is 3.6pp weaker, implying around 20% room for REER depreciation in both cases. Norway is a less conventional example: despite running a very large current-account surplus, its balance remains 2.6pp below an even larger EBA norm, producing around 27% room for depreciation relative to that benchmark. The important qualification is that the magnitude of a required FX move cannot be read from the current-account gap alone. It depends equally on how responsive trade is to the exchange rate. That distinction becomes particularly important in the tails of the distribution. It does not, by itself, tell us how the adjustment will occur. The exchange rate is one possible channel through which the current account gap can narrow over time, but it competes with fiscal policy, private saving, domestic investment, consumption, commodity prices and domestic and external financing conditions. This exercise deliberately closes those other channels and asks a narrower counterfactual: how much real exchange-rate adjustment would be required if FX had to close the external gap through trade flows alone? To quantify how strong that trade channel is, we build a trade elasticity model (see, The MS Trade Elasticity Model: Long-run, Economy-Specific and Price Aware) for 30 economies that estimates, for each economy, how far real export and import volumes could eventually move (long-run elasticity) in response to a sustained change in the real exchange rate. Isolating this response requires separating the currency from the other forces that move trade at the same time: for instance, a pickup in global demand that lifts exports regardless of price, a domestic spending boom that pulls in imports, supply chains that make imports and exports rise together, or a commodity upswing that raises export values and the currency at once. The export equation in our model is therefore conditioned on foreign demand, with real imports as a global value-chain control. records.text: value We see a range of reasons why yields are higher and have risen by slightly more than fundamental drivers imply. At the very front end, the market is pricing a significantly more hawkish Fed path than survey-based policy expectations. We recently noted that two factors—higher vol and the shift in hedge value, which we proxy with the correlation of front-end rates and equity prices— can explain about 25-to-30bp of the 40-to-50bp market-vs-survey gap at the front end (Exhibit 5). Uncertain macro environments and diminished portfolio value are both factors that should boost bond risk premium as well. These dynamics (higher vol, diminished diversification value) have been evident for longer maturities as well amid continued supply-driven swings in energy prices (Exhibit 6 and Exhibit 7). In addition to these macro drivers, investor behavior and technical factors have likely supported, and amplified, yields’ rise. Our estimate of bond funds’ duration position relative to the Bloomberg Agg has shown a steady and significant shift underweight throughout the selloff (Exhibit 8), reaching levels that have historically seen a skew towards lower yields over the subsequent 3-to-6 months. Asset managers’ aversion to duration risk likely reflects aspects of the fundamental considerations pushing yields up—namely, limited growth risks and the elevated correlation of yields with energy prices. Most of the time, though, they follow momentum, particularly in tech. Upward momentum bias is most evident in software: Despite last week’s Open AI jitters, the price momentum bias for growth sectors (particularly tech and communication services) continues to point upward (Figure 1). Notably, our single-stock momentum model reveals that the bulk of this upward bias is concentrated within software (Figure 2). (Retail) eyes on the next opportunity within AI: Following a strong September for semiconductors (SMH +9.4%), and amid increasing political scrutiny around AI data centers ahead of the US midterm elections, we anticipate retail traders may seek opportunistic MoMo trades within the AI risk spectrum. Cybersecurity stocks (CIBR ETF) currently exhibit the strongest price momentum signals in this group, making them a compelling candidate for a MoMo-driven retail 'FOMO'. But the more telling characteristic of the second step has perhaps been a shift from unemployment to inactivity. Since 2019, the expansion of social transfers and the strong rise in remittances between 2020 and 2024 have reduced the cost of not working for many households . Fewer hours will lower potential output: hours worked by formal employees would fall by 2.3% in 2027 and by around 11% by 2030 if firms were to cut overall hours by the level implied, We assume no new hires to make up the hours, which makes the output gap less negative for a given level of demand. To translate fewer hours into potential output, we weight the potential fall in formal hours by their share in the total hours worked and by the contribution of labor to output – then feed the resulting change in the output gap through our Phillips curve. With a flat Phillips curve, this channel adds less than 0.1pp a year to services inflation between 2027 and 2030. The direct increase in labor costs, by contrast, passes through to prices regardless of the state of the cycle. Its reach is limited because formal private-sector employees account for 47% of labor income in services, and firms are unlikely to pass the full cost on to prices . Our estimates exclude spillovers to informal wages or to input costs from other sectors, which would add to the effect. Under our central assumptions, with half of the cost passed through, the cost channel adds around 0.14pp to services inflation in 2027, rising to around 0.2pp a year by 2030, between three and nine times the effect of the slack channel. Compounding these pressures, we and the market expect growth to slow into 2027. Fiscal arithmetic can differ from political calculus. High real rates raise the government’s interest bill, while slower growth weakens revenues and worsens the denominator of the debt-to-GDP ratio. If fiscal uncertainty pushes risk premia higher, the BRL weakens and inflation expectations rise, leaving the BCB with limited room to ease even as activity slows. Fiscal policy, monetary policy and currency moves can then reinforce one another. From a market perspective, however, immediate fiscal balance is often not required. A clear, credible plan that convinces investors debt will eventually stabilize is often sufficient. The complication is that reforms that would most clearly change the trajectory—slower growth in mandatory expenditures, reduced indexation and greater budget flexibility—are also among the most politically challenging. A center-right Congress might find a path to such reforms, but building a durable coalition seems difficult. The economies that return an unexpected export elasticity are better understood as a group than individually. Among the more diversified commodity-exposed exporters, for example, South Africa, Indonesia and Malaysia, the export response is strong and statistically significant, because a substantial share of their exports are manufactured goods that compete on price. Among the concentrated commodity exporters, like the Latin American economies, by contrast, the export elasticity is close to zero (and statistically insignificant): these economies sell into world markets at dollar prices, so their export volumes are governed by capacity and global demand rather than by their own currency. Sweden's estimate is not statistically significant; its exports are concentrated in differentiated, high-value goods with considerable pricing power and substantial foreign-currency invoicing, so krona movements pass through only weakly to the prices foreign buyers face. records.text: AI, Credit, and a Higher Cost of Capital Questions around the funding requirements of the AI capex buildout have become more pressing, leading to a correction across risk assets. In credit, the impact has been most pronounced in USD HY. USD HY AI-related spreads widened by 25bp between October 13 and 14, reaching a new high of 360bp over Treasuries (Exhibit 1). By contrast, non-AI-related spreads were only 2bp wider and remain below their March peak. Within AI-related issuers, the widening has been concentrated in AI-related corporate bonds and data center project finance (Exhibit 2). While some softer AI-related sentiment can move datacenter bonds wider, especially if there is a reassessment around off-taker credit risk, we view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate. This is not surprising. However, for economies where the sustainable external position is materially different from zero, it can alter the magnitude of the required FX adjustment dramatically and in some cases reverse the direction of that adjustment as well. (Exhibit 25 ) Norway serves a clear illustration: Norway runs an underlying current-account surplus of 15.3% of GDP, but its EBA CA norm is even larger at 17.9%. Relative to that norm, the external position is therefore 2.6pp weak, implying that a 27% depreciation could be needed to raise the current account position further toward its EBA norm. A zero-current- account benchmark produces the exact opposite conclusion: eliminating Norway's entire surplus would require a very large appreciation, with the estimate reaching our +50% cap. Though neither calculation is arithmetically inconsistent, it imposes significantly different directions as well as magnitudes for the FX adjustment. India provides a similarly useful example from a CA deficit angle: Its current account is in a modest 0.7% deficit, but the EBA CA norm allows for a substantially larger deficit of 2.3% of GDP. records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Overproduction is the new norm: As we laid out in our previous outlook, dated 20 May, overproduction of battery cells has been a constant theme playing out in 2026, where first-use demand (from cathode producers) comfortably exceeds end-use demand.We attribute this to three key catalysts: 1) The end of the Chinese export tax rebate by end-2026 which has caused an influx of overseas cathode orders . 2) Frontloading by project developers in the EU before “Made in EU” requirements set out in the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) limit the usage of Chinese-made batteries. In H1 2026, we saw battery exports from China to Europe rising by 33% y/y. 3) Bullish sentiment on end-use demand growth fuelling the bullwhip effect across the supply chain. This led to our estimate of the difference between first-use demand and end-use demand surging to 536kt LCE, or an overproduction factor (first-use/end-use) of 1.32 in 2026. For comparison, we estimate a 136kt LCE gap in 2025, or an overproduction factor of 1.11. Due for a correction: We also mentioned, though, that we think such a phenomenon is unsustainable without equally strong growth in end-use sectors. Despite disappointing Chinese macro data, one of the more striking developments this year has been the resilience of the yuan. As the 2nd best performing Asian currency ytd, CNY has delivered ~5% in total return s, while implied volatility has fallen toward multi-decade lows (Figure 2). This resilience has come despite an increasingly K-shaped growth backdrop, where exports and AI -related investment remain strong, while consumption, fiscal spending and credit demand continue to lag. More importantly, the relationship between Chinese exports and the currency appears to have structurally changed. Historically, China’s manufacturing model was heavily concentrated in lower -value, price-sensitive exports, making a competitive currency impo rtant for preserving margins. That relationship has weakened considerably post-Covid (Figure 3). As China moved further up the value chain and expanded its role across global supply chains, export performance appears increasingly less dependent on currency depreciation. The result is greater policy tolerance for a stronger yuan without necessarily sacrificing export competitiveness. This shift is consistent with the PBoC’s recent RMB report. The central bank has emphasized that longer -term exchange rates should reflect trade balances and capital flows rather than predetermined currency levels, while explicitly pushing back against the idea of competitive devaluation. Forecast surveys are useful because revisions capture changes in the information set before realized macro data fully reflect them. The mechanics: ensembling sources by revision leadership The underlying macro forecasts framework consolidates economic forecasts from a broad set of providers, including Bloomberg, IMF, Focus Economics, Oxford Economics, country-specific central bank and survey forecasts, and internal forecasts. These forecasts arrive in different formats and horizons (current year, next year, fiscal year, end-period, annual average, rolling 12-month forecasts, etc.), so they are first mapped into a common taxonomy and converted into point-in-time fixed 12-month-ahead forecasts using Knuppel-Vladu’s fixed horizon approximation.1 This common-horizon framework separates genuine forecast revisions from mechanical effects such as calendar roll, changes in horizon definitions, and shifts in source coverage or composition. Copper Alone Is Not the Rescue Story Investors often view higher copper prices as unequivocally bullish for CLP, but the relationship is more nuanced. Chile produces about a quarter of global copper, yet imports nearly all of its energy, so rising copper and oil prices pull the currency in opposite directions (Figure 2); a sufficiently large oil shock can more than offset the positive effect of higher copper prices. Oil prices tend to quickly affect inflation, real incomes and confidence, while declining copper output has limited the boost to real GDP, which measures volumes rather than prices. Moreover, much of the copper price windfall flows to fiscal revenues, external balances and foreign mining investors rather than domestic demand. Higher copper prices remain positive for Chile’s long -term fiscal outlook, external position and growth potential, but oil could still be the more important near-term driver of CLP. If they are concentrated primarily among midstream cathode manufacturers, a slowdown in end-use procurement would likely have a substantial impact on production, as manufacturers would need to first deplete their existing inventories. This creates a vicious circle, where falling lithium prices result in a decrease in mark-to-market cathode inventory value, leading to a further rush to deplete stocks. Lithium carbonate makes up around 60-70% of LFP cathode costs, while lithium hydroxide accounts for around 30% of high nickel NMC cathode costs, according to Wood Mackenzie, making cathode manufacturers price sensitive. However, if midstream manufacturers instead face a backlog of binding orders, cathode manufacturing could remain robust for longer to fulfil previous orders, even if downstream procurement slows. We are leaning towards the former scenario, as production currently exceeds sales (see Global passenger EV sales: Staying resilient,dated 10 Sept), leading to our bearish forecast for 2027. Two other well-known examples include the ‘dash for cash’ in 2020 and LDI stress in 2022. There are a number of solutions being discussed. These broadly include: 1) better data and surveillance, 2) central clearing for cash and repo, 3) minimum haircuts, and 4) credible central bank backstops. The first three measures are intended to improve the resilience of the system in the event of a shock, rather than directly targeting a specific counterparty or level of leverage. Clearing will reduce counterparty risk and introduce netting efficiencies. Margin and haircut practices conversely will dampen the excessive build-up of leverage. In the US , the market is working towards the 2027 deadline for mandatory clearing of eligible UST transactions. In the UK, the BoE has been consulting on central clearing and haircuts with potential policy proposals due in early 2027 . These reforms are complex, given the need to assess the trade -offs between calibration and market impact. As a result, they will take time to implement. Ultimately, t his still leaves markets reliant on central bank backstops during periods of severe stress. Option-implied risk premium The hypothesis: more option compensation is bullish for carry Option markets embed both the price of protection and the perceived asymmetry of risks. When implied volatility stands well above realized volatility, investors are paying a significant premium to hedge downside outcomes. Risk reversals provide a complementary signal by capturing whether protection is more expensive against currency depreciation than appreciation. Together, these measures gauge the degree of market pessimism priced into FX options. When option compensation is unusually high, sentiment is typically skewed bearish, creating conditions for a contrarian rebound in carry returns (see Global FX weekly: Paying top dollar 25 September 2026). -6 -4 -2 0 2 4 6 8 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Aver

What comes out is the real appreciation or depreciation required to close the gap through trade competitiveness alone. That said, before we present the methodology behind this exercise and our results, allow us to list some properties of this measure for how it should be read: • It is a counterfactual measure rather than a forecast, the other adjustment channels are not shut in reality; we shut them to isolate a magnitude. • Since it is partial equilibrium, the estimates are not multilaterally consistent. We treat the required real appreciation or depreciation as a diagnostic of how asymmetrically the adjustment burden falls on FX rather than as an estimation error. • The elasticity is as informative as the required FX adjustment. Given our thesis of a capex super-cycle for Asia, investors have also been asking if higher rates will affect the funding. Our perspective is that Asia’s corporate capex is more bank-funded than capital markets, market-based rates have not gone up as much, and Asia has been funding more domestically rather than relying on external sources. Finally, while credit growth has picked up to an 18-year high, loan to deposit ratios remain healthy, suggesting there is still room to expand credit further. Which economies are more exposed to elevated US rates? As highlighted earlier, while Asia as a region is better positioned, there are still some economies in the region that are, on a relative basis, more exposed than others. Our usual framing around this issue usually revolves around rate differentials, starting point and outlook for the current account, dollar debt exposure, starting point of inflation and by extension real rates as well as the leverage situation. However, the first two – rate differentials with the US and current account balances – tend to be the key deciding factors, especially from a market perspective.

records.text: Asia Economics Week Ahead 15 October 2026 Citi Research 2 Takeaways from IMF/WB meetings, Bangkok, Day 2 Pakistan – Improved external position with likely SBP bias to pause in Oct Pakistan’s FX reserves are at an all-time high of $21.5bn (3M of imports), and Saudi financing support appears to have been extended. We previously thought that the $3bn Eurobond issuance that helped boost reserves in early September would be drained to repay Saudi short-term financing (secured back in April following UAE’s withdrawal). This seems no longer the case. It appears that of the $17.5b principal repayments scheduled for FY27 (Jul 2026 to Jun 2027), $7.3bn are to be rolled over by bilaterals (including for the Saudi financing), that “initial Saudi support had been extended for three years up to 2028” and that Pakistan is “not in a rush” to repay it. Of the remaining $10.2bn of principal repayments, $4.7bn was repaid in 1Q27 and thus Pakistan is in a comfortable position with only $5.5bn to be repaid over the course of 9M (Oct-Jun). The SBP remains confident that the current account deficit can remain contained (0-1% of its FY27 GDP forecast), notwithstanding the Middle East shock, with the help of more-buoyant-than- expected remittances, which it hopes to sustain through the launch of the Pasban Remittance Rewards Scheme (PRRS). Pakistan accessing a US$10bn US Treasury swap facility looks unlikely to us, with the US-Pakistan discussions now couched more broadly around trade and investments

records.text: 12 October 2026 Germany Schnappschuss Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Put together, the consensus implies a peculiar AI scenario: the technology is powerful enough to sustain a global investment and asset-price boom, but not powerful enough to deliver meaningful productivity gains in Germany by 2030. That is not impossible. Germany could be slow to capture the gains, or other headwinds could offset some of them. But if the scale of today's AI build-out is broadly justified by the technology's transformative potential, it is hard to see Germany receiving no productivity benefit at all by the end of the decade, even allowing for a ‘J-curve’ (the usual lag before adoption pays off). The alternative is that AI is simply not powerful enough to raise productivity growth noticeably. But then the global capex boom itself becomes more vulnerable next year. As new data centers come on stream and onto balance sheets, investors will increasingly expect revenues commensurate with the scale of investment. If those disappoint, the boom could deflate substantially, and global growth could roll over quickly, derailing Germany's recovery from abroad despite strong fiscal stimulus at home. The institutes' latest joint forecast does acknowledge cyclical downside risks from a decelerating AI boom. But the medium-term projection allows for no structural upside risk from what could be one of the most transformative technologies in human history. It would not be inconsistent to stress both risks.
