records.text: Brazil Equities: Benchmarking the Election Rally; Scope for Further Gains if Policy Delivers Brazilian assets have seen sharp moves following the first round of general election, which saw conservative right gaining political strength in Brazil. Since the first round of elections, the Brazilian real has strengthened, local rates have moved significantly lower and equities have rallied sharply consistent with our views coming into the election. In this Global Markets Daily, we focus on equities and assess how much further upside could Brazilian equities see on favorable policy delivery, benchmarking the current rally to its prior election cycles and other market-friendly election outcomes in EM and highlight pockets that appear best placed to position for further upside. Higher rates have weakened affordability—not household solvency Higher rates are testing household affordability, but have not materially impaired aggregate solvency. This is a caution signal, not a recession signal. The SCF provides the structural explanation. Aggregate consumer health deteriorated modestly from 2022 to 2025, yet the -0.5 z-score remains the second strongest reading since 1995. The deterioration came through rising debt payments to income, which offset modest improvements in debt to net worth and debt to income. Moderate debt growth and substantial asset appreciation have strengthened household net worth, particularly among upper-income cohorts. By contrast, debt-payment burdens rose across every income cohort as interest rates normalized higher. That cushion has become less reliable in recent months. Since July, USD and EUR credit spreads have moved higher in tandem with government yields, creating a dual headwind for unhedged credit returns. In this Global Markets Daily, we revisit the relationship between rates and credit n spreads, focusing on why the correlation has shifted into more positive territory and what that means for credit investors. The spread/rates correlation is especially important for IG credit, where elevated all-in yields have been an important technical support for demand in recent years. In USD IG, credit spreads account for less than 15% of all-in yield today, versus an average of 45% between 2019 and 2021. BAPT is not a measure of realised ASPs, company inventory or sales performance. Rather, it provides a consistent view of distributor-channel trends that can help identify developing industry dynamics before they become visible in reported results. Data Science & Applied AI – Methodology Vincenzo Pota(iii) Barclays, UK Methodology The analysis tracks semiconductor product pricing and inventory across distributors on a weekly basis. The pricing data was scraped from six websites, from which we extracted the product identifier, price, currency and the stock number. Each week we scrape roughly 300k distinct SKUs. The raw data were cleaned and standardised using the python language. Most products are listed in USD, but a few might have foreign currencies. We convert all products to point-in-time USD. Each product’s available inventory was calculated by multiplying its average price and units in stock, aggregated by product category and company. Company- and category-level pricing metrics were calculated as equal-weighted averages across observed products, whereas we use weighted average for the overall price trend. records.text: M Idea 6 Lead 1) Will lead remain oversupplied? Although lead mine supply has come under pressure alongside zinc (-4% YTD), the lead market has remained well supplied, with weak demand and support from secondary availability. China looks relatively strong for end demand, with lead-acid battery imports up 94% YoY in August. Treatment charges have seen a similar fate to copper and zinc, falling into negative territory, reflective of tight mine supply. 2) Can positioning fall further? Lead short positions held by investment funds have reached record highs, pushing net short positioning to a record level too, even as longs remain elevated. Lead's 50-day moving average (dma) crossed below its 100 dma in July, a bearish signal that can drive selling by CTA traders. This has weighed on pricing too, although lead seems to be finding some support between $1,850 and $1,900/t. If anything does drive lead pricing higher, this positioning could be caught offside and forced to cover. 3) What are the risks? Lead prices and demand can see some seasonality, with replacement battery demand usually strongest in the Northern Hemisphere winter. China's demand has shown some demand strength with a jump in battery imports, and inventories are low, while LME inventories are also drawing, albeit from high levels. In the first half of the trading session on Monday and again on Thursday, the USD sold off on risk-off and US rates rallied. We think this reflects the nature of the risk-off as related to concerns about AI-related earnings rather than being driven by energy or rates. Over recent months, foreign equity inflows into the US have accelerated, at the expense of debt buying. Last year was the first year where equity and debt inflows were roughly even. These large accumulated holdings from foreign investors could leave the USD vulnerable in an AI-led risk-off. For the majority of this year, it has been challenging to observe a clear catalyst for AI momentum to turn. We think this could change heading into the US midterm elections. One consequence of prolonged easing has been a weakening in the carry appeal of EM currencies, with the aggregate carry-to- volatility profile deteriorating gradually in recent years (Figure 2). Assuming volatility remains contained, a significant assumption should markets weaken anew, the shift back towards rate hikes should improve the carry-to-volatility profile of higher-yielding EM currencies. Yet the carry argument cannot be considered independently of valuation and positioning. High yields are less compelling if currencies are already expensive and investors overweight. Notably, few currencies currently satisfy both conditions. Figure 3 illustrates EM FX REER relative to their 10-year history. The results are striking: undervaluation is concentrated almost entirely in lower yielding Emerging Asian currencies. In contrast, overvaluation is concentrated in Emerging EMEA and LatAm, suggesting that their traditionally more attractive yield profiles have come at the expense of increasingly stretched valuations. Import Equation: Absorption, Activity and Currency that Sets the Price We assume import volumes are driven by two forces: domestic spending, and the price of foreign goods relative to domestic ones, measured by the real effective exchange rate. This follows the standard import demand framework in the trade literature. Houthakker and Magee (1969) first estimated import demand as a function of domestic income and relative prices. Goldstein and Khan (1985) established this income-plus- relative-price form, estimated on real volumes, as the canonical specification. We follow the literature in using a spending-based activity measure, and add the controls below to separate the effect of the exchange rate from that of demand and the commodity cycle. This is more of a thought experiment than something investors or markets should expect or like to see occur. We view this as a useful stress test and thought experiment, not as an alternative definition of equilibrium. A zero current account does not imply that an economy has reached its economically appropriate external position, nor does a persistent surplus or deficit necessarily represent a disequilibrium. For economies with structurally justified external positions, the zero-anchor calculation can therefore materially overstate the degree of FX adjustment required. We point this out in the Model Results section. records.text: M Global Foundation 20 paper, Supply Chain Strain, we argued the next phase of supply-chain reorientation will be costlier, slower and riskier, because the remaining products are complex, production is concentrated and the required capital and labour scarce. The experience of the past year has been broadly consistent with that view. In Supply Chain Reconfiguration — China, Tariffs, and AI One Year On, we characterised 2025 as a year in which headline trade volumes stayed broadly resilient while the underlying drivers became narrower, more regional and more policy-driven. US–China de-linking accelerated, but flows were largely rerouted through other economies, while production structures changed more gradually. For economies with weaker elasticities, the constraint may not only be that domestic output is too expensive, but also that it is not yet available in sufficient quantity, quality or complexity. The exchange rate still shapes the incentive to build that capacity, as a sustained real depreciation can make domestic production more profitable and support the case for capital expenditure. However, the volume response is likely to emerge over the period of capacity formation rather than at the point of price adjustment. Tariff policy can also influence trade volumes. A fall in imports may reflect domestic substitution, but it may equally reflect demand compression, inventory adjustment, rerouting through third countries or administrative restrictions. Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 14 October 2026 2 Understanding range accruals, and their impact on volatility hedging: Range accrual notes are yield-enhancement products where investors earn an above-market coupon for each day a reference rate stays inside a pre -set range, and nothing for the days it does not. Principal is returned at par. These notes are mostly issued by large banks, and usually carry a ‘call’ feature. They are bought by private-bank, retail, and institutional accounts that want carry and expect rates to stay range-bound. Mechanically, the buyer sells volatility to the issuer, and the issuer passes that to the dealer, making range accruals a recurring source of volatility supply. The investor is long a series of daily high strike digital floorlets and therefore short volatility – the value of a digital is the probability of the fixing being in the range; higher volatility only raises the probability of an ITM option ending OTM. The enhanced coupon is the premium for that short volatility position. The dealer, on the other side, is short the series of digitals and therefore long volatility. Structure and hedging: A 10y CMT range accrual note with a high strike K is a par bond plus a strip of daily digital floorlets struck at K (e.g. 5.25%). records.text: Rumblings publication was as follows: why does the share of cash and reserves in HQLA matter when government bonds are close to perfect substitutes? Shouldn't the discussion be about where the floor of cash plus government bonds in the HQLA is? In the aggregate data, if we look at the share of cash and reserves plus government bonds, the combined share of this group in the HQLA mix has fallen slightly as the HQLA rotation has ensured some degree of stability to this metric (relative to share of cash and reserves) ( Figure 8). We see a broadly similar dynamic in country-level data, although there are again some cross- country differences which account for relative preference for other HQLA assets (high-quality covered bonds, other L1 assets etc.) ( Figure 9). On the face of it, it is a fair question since banks can repo out their bond holdings to the ECB or in the market and raise cash. However, the concept of bonds being perfect substitutes is not entirely true. This is because while reserves are risk free, their value does not fluctuate and they can be used instantly for payments. However, the value of government bonds fluctuates and borrowing against these bonds at the ECB's MRO or L TRO is based on market, and not face, value. Ie, in a stressed situation, if a bank wants to convert its bonds to cash in the repo market, the cash it receives would be based on the market rather than the face value of the bond. In the context of recent client discussions amid the global rates sell- off, Brazil is an interesting case study. For investors in Brazilian assets, the fundamental question around the election is the fiscal outlook. Brazil’s fiscal space has been under pressure for many years. The headline deficit is approaching 10% of GDP, while the primary deficit is below 1%, implying a heavy interest burden that makes rates and the external balance especially important. The solutions are highly policy dependent, which explains the market focus on the election. Although markets seem to be pricing greater fiscal restraint, we do not think the outlook is quite so straightforward. In the latest rates-up-vol-up episode, intermediate-right vols/skews have broken out of the range and stayed elevated until only recently (see Figure 1). Outlook: We have seen the initial phase of the volatility pullback, as 3y10y dropped 9nvol from 106 to 97 in the five days after the peak on 5 October. In the near term, we anticipate asymmetric volatility moves, where volatility drifts gradually lower in a rally as it converges toward the regression line, and firms up more markedly in a sell-off (see Figure 2). This asymmetry stems from the negative convexity profile of dealers' exotic books, which require s them to go long volatility in a high-vol environment – a mechanism that was triggered during the latest episode and further reinforced by the additional tailwind of position liquidations. The movement in skew is expected to be more gradual, lagging the volatility move as long as underlyings stay above the strikes (see Figure 4). During this period, dealers’ hedging remains long skew, while other factors such as callable issuance provides a persistent supply of vol. Ultimately, the pace of the skew correction will likely accelerate only when underlyings breach the strikes and the underlying hedging mechanism reverses. For context, total German storage capacity is ~22 bcm and still sits at only 60% fill. So far Germany has refrained from instructing THE to purchase gas directly, as they did in 2022. Despite stronger injections through September and October, the overall European storage outlook remains largely unchanged. We still expect Europe to enter winter with inventories just 74% full, the lowest pre-winter level in our high frequency gas market data (Exhibit 2), leaving the market particularly exposed to a normal-to-cold winter. While inventories look less stretched when adjusted for lower European gas demand, we believe this benefit is largely offset by reduced supply flexibility. Europe's marginal supply now comes from LNG, with delivery lead times of 2-3 weeks versus just 2-3 days for pipeline gas pre-2022, increasing the reliance on storage to absorb short-term demand shocks. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 27 Model Results James Lord, Nimish Prabhune We present our main takeaways from the required-FX adjustment framework below. Global View: Required FX Adjustment is Two-Sided The first takeaway from the cross-country results is that there is no single global direction of required FX adjustment. Using the EBA current-account norms as our preferred benchmark, the sample remains broadly balanced: 14 currencies show upward required adjustments and 14 show downward required adjustments, with several estimates relatively close to equilibrium. What differs much more materially is the size of the adjustment. The distribution has relatively fat tails, with a number of currencies implying required REER moves of 20% or more if FX alone were tasked with closing the external imbalance. ( Exhibit 24 ) The dispersion is economically intuitive. Economies with external positions materially stronger than their EBA current-account norms tend to populate the appreciation side of the distribution, while those with external positions weaker than their norms generally show room for depreciation. The currencies that would need to appreciate the most to close the C/A gap are SEK, KRW and PEN, each reaching our +50% cap, followed by HUF (+25%), CNY (+22%) and JPY (+20%). records.text: M Idea 20 Review of supply, demand and inventories for September September was an unusually warm month across the perimeter, with heating degree days running 45% below the 10-year average and cooling degree days 49% above it. Residential and commercial heating demand fell 17% YoY as a result, helping drive a 4% decline in total gas demand YoY despite demand for power generation continuing to grow strongly. Industrial gas demand contracted for a third consecutive month in September, down 8% YoY and 8% below the three-year average, even as the euro area manufacturing PMI continued to improve, rising to 52.9 from 52.7 in August. Belgium showed the most weakness (-26% YoY), with BASF confirming it had cut run rates at a 645,000 t/yr ammonia line at its Antwerp site due to high gas costs. France also contracted sharply in September, down 14% YoY. Germany and Italy posted more moderate declines of 5% and 7% YoY respectively, while the Netherlands was flat YoY. Gas demand for power generation rose 16% YoY and ran 11% above its 3Y average, even as total power generation across the perimeter was broadly flat YoY. The gas-for- power strength in September reflects a weak hydro and nuclear backdrop. Sri Lanka — Higher-than-expected hurdle to hike; successor IMF program, no decision on MLB buyback. The CBSL seems more reluctant than expected to hike rates further following the preemptive 100bps increase in May, and given its view that inflation expectations remain well anchored. Fed policy/global rate differentials seem to matter less to the central bank, and we believe the key factor to monitor for future policy action are 1) FX pressures; and 2) credit growth. records.text: Higher yields have also brought negative convexity in MBS and Treasury futures to the fore. Decreased mortgage prepayment risk and changes to long-end futures’ cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond have boosted duration exposure for long investors since the start of September. Our estimate of the share of MBS holders that actively hedge would imply roughly $60bn in 10y equivalent paying needs through the selloff to maintain steady duration exposure since the start of September (though this is likely on the high side of realized flows). Exhibit 7: ...and geopolitical risks remain elevated, with rising tanker attacks First, freight rates and why they have risen so much Tanker rates are historically volatile but have recently risen to record highs in every size class. On several routes, rates are multiples of previous records. For example, take the route TD3C, i.e. Middle East to China, using a Very Large Crude Carrier – arguably the benchmark route for VLCCs. Over the last five years, this rate has typically been $6-22 per metric tonne. There are 7.3 barrels of crude in a tonne, so this equalled $1-3 per barrel – small relative to the price of crude. At the moment, that rate is ~$250/tonne, or ~$34/bbl. The Dubai benchmark was assessed at $110/bbl yesterday; delivered in China, this becomes $144/bbl. Several factors have come together to explain this unusual rise: • Shuttle and ship-to-ship (STS) operations use two ships per barrel, plus days of waiting. Crude oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz have increased, but the logistics of these exports are complex and inefficient. Crude is shuttled out of the Gulf and transferred in the Gulf of Oman onto ships for the onward voyage. Each transfer takes several days, and Fujairah waits can exceed 10 days. Clarksons estimates that STS waiting alone ties up about 5% of global VLCC capacity. • Voyages have become much longer. The Houthi threat closed Bab el-Mandeb

Over the summer, Italian banks have cooled their BTP purchases, broadly in line with historical seasonality, which is typically followed by net selling in Q4 (Exhibit 7). While they were net buyers of EGBs in 4Q25, their EGB holdings are now even more elevated as a share of total assets, while reserves account for an even smaller share of HQLA (see note, EGB supply, positioning & flows Oct. 2026). This arguably leaves less scope for a repeat this year. At the same time, Italian banks have continued to diversify their sovereign portfolios, gradually increasing their holdings of non-domestic EGBs, a long-running trend since the European sovereign debt crisis. However, there have been periodic deviations, in which banks have notably favoured domestic government bonds. Such episodes have coincided with a widening in BTP-Bund spreads, suggesting that Italian banks remain willing to add BTP exposure when valuations become sufficiently attractive, and to support BTP issuance when needed. records.text: Euro Area—Re fining the Energy Inflation Outlook European fuel prices have risen much more than crude oil as refining margins widened sharply. Pump prices are near historical peaks despite a smaller increase in crude than during previous energy shocks. Since February 2026, crude oil has risen around 45%, while diesel, petrol and heating oil prices were up 40%, 28% and 77%, respectively, by late September—well above their historical sensitivity to oil. Pass-through from pump prices to fuels HICP has remained broadly as expected (Exhibit 1). This unusually strong relationship between crude and refined products raises questions around forecasting fuel inflation beyond timely pump data and the reliability of our energy inflation “rules of thumb”. In this Daily, we reassess the pass-through from oil and natural gas into Euro area inflation and update our forecasting framework to reflect the greater importance of refined product spreads. We first assess transmission from crude oil to transport and liquid fuels at the pump. Rolling ten-year local projections1 show that pass-through has increased in recent years, consistent with refining margins widening alongside crude. A 10% oil price increase is now associated with an approximately 10% rise in pump heating oil prices, versus 7% historically. Pass-through to petrol and diesel has also risen, though more moderately, to around 4% and 5.5%, respectively, after just three months (Exhibit 2, left). Using the respective HICP weights and

We recommend receiving 1yf 2y SOFR rates. US Treasuries rallied sharply over the week, led by the long end, amid jitters in risk sentiment, even as the inflation print surprised to the upside. Since last Friday's close, 2y yields have fallen 4bp and 30y yields 15-20bp ( Figure 1). When foreign demand strengthens, an integrated exporter imports more inputs and exports more final output, and the exchange rate can be misattributed without controlling for this co-movement. A commodity boom can raise export production and appreciate the currency at the same time, creating a positive export-REER correlation that has nothing to do with bilateral trade flows. The expected long run export elasticity is negative: A sustained appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of domestic value added and should reduce real export volumes. Across the sample, the export response is statistically significant for most of the economies. The magnitudes follow trade structure. Export volumes are most sensitive to REER where goods compete on price at the margin, as in China and Thailand, whose manufacturers face close regional substitutes. They are least sensitive in two groups: 1) concentrated commodity exporters, whose goods are priced in dollars on world markets, so their own currency changes producer margins rather than foreign demand, and 2) economies embedded deep in regional supply chains, where the exporter is often not the price-setter and much of the value of an export is imported in the first place. records.text: sticities in the G10. Two structural features explain it. First, Japanese manufacturers have built production abroad for decades. Japan is the largest source of foreign direct investment in the US, so the current-account surplus rests on overseas income receipts more than on trade, and a weaker yen lifts the yen value of those earnings more than export volumes. Second, the marginal import bill is energy and food, which respond little to price, so a weaker yen raises its cost without reducing the quantity. The terms of trade, rather than volumes, are therefore the margin of adjustment, where the AI cycle has started to help, with strong global AI-related demand lifting export prices enough to offset part of the oil-driven rise in import costs. Our FX strategists see those same forces keeping the yen weak: with Brent prices volatile and households' steady foreign-equity buying through NISA, large-scale repatriation looks unlikely, so recent JPY strength reflects speculative carry unwinding rather than a change in fundamentals. Japan does not disprove the trade channel, it localises it. The yen is being set by the energy bill and the financial account rather than by trade volumes, and the route to a more responsive import side runs through domestic energy and manufacturing capacity, not through the exchange rate.

records.text: Rates and equity vol support for FX, dated 7 February 2022). This year, the spillover from other asset classes to FX vol has generally been low. Geopolitical risks have spurred higher energy prices and rising volatility across the commodity complex, but spillover analysis indicates that the impulse from higher commodity vol to FX vol has diminished. Figure 3 plots spillover of 3m Brent vol to 3m EURUSD: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 saw Brent vol drove EURUSD vol higher (labelled ‘1’ in Figure 3) but spillover from subsequent spikes in the oil price (labelled ‘2’ and ‘3’) has diminished. Geopolitical risk spillover to FX vol has fallen. To some extent, low spillover created a feedback loop through the middle of this year: low realised vol and tight ranges discouraged option ownership, and overall FX option volumes fell (Figure 4) – in EURUSD, volumes halved from the January peak to the July low. However, spillover from rates vol has risen, and FX options trading volumes have now increased. Figure 5 plots the spillover coefficient of US 3m10y rates vol to EURUSD and Japanese 3m1y rates vol to USDJPY: the former is at its highest level since January; the latter is at its highest level since the pandemic. Higher rates vol is leading to higher FX vol. We think the reason for higher rates vol – fiscal sustainability concerns – could persist, particularly for the EUR, where fiscal sustainability may remain a key theme until next year’s French presidential election.

Its import elasticity rises from an insignificant +0.093 on the REER to +0.131 on the invoicing-weighted rate. Central Europe shows that composition, not just invoicing, determines the strength of the import response. Romania, Czechia, Poland and Hungary all invoice predominantly in euros and trade predominantly with the euro area, so the two measures largely coincide and the invoicing correction adds little. Their import elasticities nonetheless differ sharply. Romania's response is among the strongest in the sample on either measure. Its imports are driven by consumption, financing a current-account deficit of around 7.5% of GDP, and its import basket leans toward cars, consumer durables and processed goods for final use, which respond to relative prices. The CE3 economies import mainly components and intermediate goods that are assembled and re-exported within euro-area supply chains, so their imports follow the export cycle rather than the currency, and the elasticity is low on either measure. Although front-end rates are increasingly skewed to the downside, energy-price volatility and related monetary policy uncertainty remain high. The clearest route to a near-term peak in global yields would be tighter financial conditions weighing on growth sentiment; recent pressure in corporate and sovereign credit suggests the bond sell-off may be approaching a speed limit. Increasing EU sovereign spreads also created demand for relative safe havens such as US Treasuries and German bunds. Even with persistent uncertainty over equilibrium yields, bonds should gradually move from a portfolio headwind towards becoming a more effective hedge. The ongoing AI capex boom and its financing needs, alongside lingering fiscal concerns, have increased uncertainty around the medium-term fair value of bond yields. However, higher carry and reinvestment yields should cushion the impact of further rate increases. As Exhibit 11 shows, higher starting yields give long-duration bonds better asymmetry for longer investment horizons: potential gains from rate relief now exceed the likely losses from a further rise in yields. The USD is smiling again After the brief disruption caused by the Iran war in March, asset managers embarked on a 108-day run of broad-based risk seeking, captured by our Behavioural Risk Scorecard. Since that run ended on 3 September, conditions have become much trickier: equities and bonds have fallen, and investors have spent the past two weeks cutting risk. The consolation is that, rather than retreating to cash, they are again finding value in US Treasuries—and rediscovering the USD. Dollar buying during risk-off periods is familiar, but April/May 2025 showed it cannot be taken for granted. So far in 2026, the USD “smile” —the dollar rallying in strong risk-on or risk-off regimes—appears intact. Twenty-day asset- manager inflows are near a five-year high as investors de-risk (Figure 1). OUR KEY VIEWS ▪ We anticipate asymmetric volatility moves from here: a slow drift lower in a rally, and a more marked firming up in a sell-off, with skew following the move with a lag. ▪ Our view follows the latest vol-up episode led by the rates sell-off, which has seen intermediate- right vols and skews corrected at a much slower pace, standing out from earlier episodes. ▪ We think this is due to dealers’ exotic books becoming more short vega in a sell-off – and the ensuing hedging activity reinforcing volatility higher. Market trends and t he recent sell -off: Since H2 2024, USD range accrual issuance has seen a resurgence, and accelerated significantly in 2026, with some sizable issuance clustered around the 5% strike . Under this backdrop , the rates vol market has experienced one of the sharpest price actions since Covid – even more than the peak due to the Iran war (see Figures 1 and 2). The sharp rise in yield is fuelled by a confluence of macro and technical factors (see US rates: Don’t fade this, dated 23 September, and US rates: Rise of the Planet of the Rates, dated 28 September). The rise in yield pushed these range accrual notes from in-the-money (ITM) to out-of-the-money (OTM). In the latest rates-up-vol-up episode, intermediate-right vols/skews have broken out of the range and stayed elevated until only recently (see Figure 1).

Fiscal outturns: Public-sector net borrowing and the central government net cash requirement are tracking higher than the OBR’s March projections, according to monthly public finance data (Figure 5). While PSNB has overshot expectations by GBP8.1bn, the impact on CGNCR has been limited to GBP3.0bn. On both metrics, the overshoot primarily reflects the impact of higher interest expenditure from the RPI-linked bonds referred to above. We assume this overshoot persists and captures some of the increase in debt-interest spending. Buffering factors: In our projections, additional spending is partially offset by higher revenues from the Energy Profits Levy and the Electricity Generator Levy, higher revenues from Capital Gains Tax due to the better-than-expected performance of UK equities, and the stabilisation of the UK labour market limiting the need for cyclical stabilisers (see appendix and Reports of the death of the UK labour market may be exaggerated, dated 21 July). The OBR’s assessment of whether recent economic performance is driven by demand or supply is crucial for the fiscal outlook. Whereas demand-led growth may offer only a temporary boost, supply-side improvements could provide a more durable medium-term tailwind for fiscal forecasts. records.text: be we already have Much has been made of the "normalization" of interest rates in recent weeks, months and quarters, but one thing that has not normalized is medium-term market-based measures of inflation compensation; namely the closely watched 5y5y CPI swap rate. From 2004 through 2013, the median 5y5y CPI swap rate was 2.91%, c.50bp above current levels ( Figure 1). If one thinks of medium-term inflation risk premium as market pricing relative to levels consistent with the Fed's target, this would imply 50-60bp of inflation risk premium on average from 2004 to 2013. By contrast, with 5y5y CPI swaps currently at c.2.4%, one could argue there is little to no inflation risk premium, at least relative to "target-consistent" levels. At first pass, it is compelling to argue that if rates normalize, inflation risk premium could as well, and therefore there could be c.50bp of upside risk to medium- and long-term breakevens and CPI swap rates. 15 October 2026 8 FICC Research Interest Rates 15 October 2026 Jonathan Hill, CFA +1 212 526 3497 jonathan.hill@barclays.com BCI, US Apostolos Apostolou +1 212 526 5051 apostolos.apostolou@barclays.com BCI, US

Rather than maintaining a constant allocation through time, the sentiment overlay scales both the direction and magnitude of exposure according to prevailing macro and market conditions. Our backtest specifications are as follows: • The backtest uses weekly observations of the Sentiment Indicator and monthly rebalancing. • The indicator is scaled continuously between fully bullish (-1) and fully bearish (+1). • Readings above +0.5 correspond to maximum long exposure, while readings below -0.5 correspond to maximum short exposure. • Intermediate readings scale portfolio exposure proportionally. • Portfolio decisions are made at month-end and implemented using the first available return date thereafter. • Transaction costs of 10bp per 1x one-way turnover are applied whenever positions change. All reported results are net of transaction costs. We evaluate four portfolio variants (see Exhibit 19). For a worker above the limit, the cost increase depends on how the employer responds. As the legislation dictates that weekly pay cannot fall if hours need to be reduced, the cost per hour rises in proportion to the hours lost: a worker going from 48 to 46 hours becomes about 4% more expensive per hour. If the employer maintains a worker’s hours and pays the excess as overtime at double the ordinary rate, the wage bill rises by twice the excess hours relative to the new limit . We aggregate using wages as weights, so the results measure the cost to employers, with higher-paid workers weighing more . The survey records hours actually worked, which can differ from contractual hours, so the estimates are an approximation . If firms cut current workers’ hours and keep pay unchanged, the hourly cost of labor in formal services rises by 1.7% in 2027 and by 9.2% cumulatively by 2030. If they keep all workers on their current hours and pay the excess as overtime, at double the ordinary rate, the increase is 3.4% in 2027 and 18.3% by 2030. Both figures are upper bounds. In practice, firms are likely to combine both responses and offset part of the cost through new hires, reorganization, productivity gains or lower margins. Two broader measures capture the rest of the slack. ‘Underemployment’ covers people who have a job, but who want more hours and are available to work them. A third group covers those who are available to work but have stopped searching. All three combine to produce a labor underutilization rate that was about 17% in Q2 2026, several times greater than the unemployment rate. Recessions show up more in hours, participation: Mexico has no national unemployment insurance. Formal employees who lose their jobs can withdraw only a limited share of their pension savings, and informal workers – more than half of the employed – have no protection at all. A worker who loses a formal job therefore tends to take whatever work is available, often an informal job or one with fewer hours than desired, which raises underemployment. Those who cannot find work worth taking stop searching and are counted as being outside the labor force; whether they leave for good depends largely on other sources of household income, a point we return to when discussing the NAIRU. This is an important part of the global-rebalancing debate: the effectiveness of FX depends on whether firms and consumers are actually able to respond to the change in relative prices. We translate these country-specific trade responses into required REER adjustments using two inputs: the size of the external imbalance and the sensitivity of the trade balance to FX. Our preferred benchmark is the IMF's External Balance Assessment current-account norm. A sustainable current account need not be zero: demographics, growth prospects, net foreign assets and other structural characteristics can justify persistent surpluses in some economies and deficits in others. We also calculate the move required to take the current account to zero, but regard this primarily as a stress test. That distinction matters. Norway runs a very large current-account surplus, but its sustainable current account position is larger still; relative to that benchmark, FX depreciation rather than appreciation would be required. India runs a current-account deficit, but one that is smaller than its fundamentals can sustain, implying appreciation required to push the current account to its sustainable level. The sign of the headline current account is therefore not sufficient to tell investors which way FX would need to move to facilitate external adjustment. What Do The Global Results Suggest? In addition, the widest implied crosses are not always the most liquid or practical to trade, so the matrix should often be read as a bilateral diagnostic rather than a direct implementation guide. In addition, the bilateral reconstruction also inherits the guardrails applied to the underlying REER estimates. In particular, required REER adjustments are capped at ±50%, so the resulting bilateral matrix should be interpreted as internally consistent with the reported, winsorised REER adjustments, rather than with potentially more extreme unconstrained model-implied adjustments. We are candid that this framework sits closer to a controlled thought experiment than to a valuation tool. It holds every adjustment channel but the currency shut in order to isolate a magnitude, and identifies where FX is a weak instrument for closing it. Our published FX fair value estimates continue to rest on the FEER and BEER frameworks, which are built for that purpose. We present the latest fair value estimates from our FEER model in the next section.

records.text: Please ref er to important inf ormation at the end of the report and MAR disclosures The equilibrium rate of unemployment has fallen: The NAIRU, the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, cannot be observed directly. We estimate it together with the output gap. When unemployment falls, we ask whether the economy was running hot enough to explain the decline – if it was, the fall is cyclical, if it was not, it is attributed to a lower equilibrium rate. The NAIRU held at around 5% between 2008 and 2013, fell to around 3.9% by 2018 and declined again after the pandemic, to around 2.6% in Q2 2026 (see Figure 4). Measured against it, the labor market was tight in 2016–19 and has moved into mild slack since 2025 (see Figure 6). A two-step fall: The first step lower in the NAIRU ran from 2013 to 2018 and the second from 2021 to 2026, after a period of stability in 2018 –20. The first step coincided with the 2012 labor reform and came in a period characterised by an aging labor force. The reform, enacted from December 2012, introduced trial periods, initial-training contracts and hourly hiring, which may have lowered the cost of hiring and shortened job search. Demographics were pushing in the same direction: younger workers change jobs more often, so as the labor force ages the aggregate unemployment rate falls. The more important question, in our view, is whether this reflects a temporary response to a rapid rates repricing or a more persistent change in the macro backdrop for credit. That distinction is particularly relevant given the importance of elevated all-in yields for credit demand in both USD and EUR IG credit markets. Oil, Fiscal Risks, and the Speed of the Move Help Explain the Shift Historically, the relationship between rates and spreads has been state-dependent. In a benign scenario of a positive growth shock, higher government yields can coincide with tighter spreads, as stronger growth supports corporate earnings and reduces downside macro risks. By contrast, in inflationary or fiscal shocks, both rates and spreads can sell off together. Two features of the recent macro backdrop help explain the latest move. First, the spread/rates correlation becomes less negative as oil prices rise. Higher energy prices make a rise in government yields more inflationary and less benign for credit, particularly where higher input costs and weaker real income growth may weigh on the growth outlook (Exhibit 3). Second, spread/rates correlations tend to turn positive when the rise in Treasury or Bund yields is rapid. The speed of the move matters because it gives investors less time to distinguish between a benign rise in yields associated with stronger growth and a more adverse move

We therefore test whether the Sentiment Indicator can improve the performance of practical EMFX carry strategies. Benchmark portfolios: vanilla EMFX and carry strategies The backtest starts with constructing two portfolios that serve as our buy-and-hold benchmarks and represent simple ways of harvesting the carry risk premium without any macro timing overlay. The first is an equal-weight portfolio, which allocates the same weight to every active currency in the universe. records.text: Global Strategy 12 October 2026 ab 12 US Credit Strategy: Strong Demand Absorbs Rising AI Debt Supply, but Dispersion Is Widening • Do not overstate the crowding-out risk from heavy corporate supply: Higher Treasury yields appear driven more by resilient growth, global fiscal concerns and geopolitics than corporate issuance itself. • Higher rates have already reshaped borrower behavior: IG issuers have responded to higher yields by shifting supply toward shorter maturities and less discretionary supply. • Stay selective on AI debt: repeat issuers are paying wider concessions, but demand remains healthy across markets. We favor credit selection in HY Datacenter credits where investor differentiation is most pronounced and see room for IG tech curves to steepen into 2027. • Stay underweight Private Credit vs. stronger public market opportunities: BDC non-accruals remain elevated and bankruptcy trends in technology, services and healthcare continue to rise despite some easing in aggregate private-company filings. Expect greater dispersion across private-credit managers and portfolios. • AI Disruption is more a leveraged software problem than a blanket short: Software remains the most exposed segment, while business services have proved more resilient. Evidence of disruption is more consistent with pricing-power pressure than universal business-model obsolescence.

In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise the costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline, as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich, and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real-time information on consumer behaviour. records.text: M Global Idea 2 Exceptional Shipping Cost and Its Impact on Brent Prices With Hormuz flows sharply increased, why is crude still $100? Over the last ~4 weeks, crude oil exports from the Middle East have sharply increased again. Taking into account all routes, exports are within 10-15% of pre-conflict levels – from 7-8 mb/d earlier on in the crisis, to 15-16 mb/d recently. But despite such a large increase in supply, the front-month Brent future has remained robust at over $100/bbl – this raises the question: why? Several factors play a role: • First, total supply has not recovered yet: Exports may be up, but total supply to the market – i.e. including into domestic refineries – is still tracking well below last year's levels. This is not only an issue in the Middle East but in Russia too. Taking the seven impacted countries in the Middle East Gulf and Russia combined, total crude supply was ~29.5 mb/d in September, according to Petro-Logistics data, still down 5.5 mb/d year-on-year. • Second, onshore crude oil inventories are low and still falling: Oil-on-water has recently increased, but land-based crude oil inventories continue to decline steadily, and are now at multi-year lows. • Third, geopolitical risks stay high: The number of tanker attacks has notably increased again. There were typically 2-3.5 tanker attacks per week during July and August. The takeaway for investors follows intuitively; the argument that medium-term CPI pricing should be higher just because it used to be weakens under scrutiny. To be sure, there are other reasons that both baseline inflation expectations and inflation risk premium could be arguably higher now than pre-GFC (namely sovereign debt levels, the risk that elevated inflation will be required to inflate away the debt, a structural energy supply/demand mismatch, etc.) but that is for a different conversation. Dashed line is pre-2014 median. Source: Bloomberg, SPF, Macrobond, Barclays Research Waking up from the American dream in a rental Higher mortgage payments to higher rents? With 30y mortgage rates having risen nearly 150bp since early March, it is reasonable to ponder whether this presents upside risk to the more relevant shelter price metric for CPI: rents. At a high level, the two should be related; when a household is deciding between renting or buying, presumably it would compare monthly mortgage payments with monthly rent payments (as a key factor among several). When mortgage payments are rising, that should dis-incentivize buying a home, reducing ownership demand, but increasing rental demand, and thus putting upward pressure on rental prices. 15 October 2026 10 Barclays

records.text: M Idea 4 The European Balance Remains Fragile A Small September Boost from Warm Weather A mild start to winter, government backed gas buying and minimal Norwegian maintenance over September have combined to give Europe's gas inventories a final boost into the end of the filling season. Storage injection rates in our perimeter averaged +35% above the 5Y average over the last 6 weeks. We now model a 74% end- October inventory fill level in our perimeter, vs our previous estimate of 71%. Weak gas demand under a mild autumn was the major driver of strong injections. Over September and early October, gas demand has been running ~12% lower YoY in our European perimeter, driven by weak residential commercial heating and industrial gas demand. Gas for power demand has continued to offset weakness in these sectors, as both gas and coal continue to be utilised to offset weak nuclear and hydro demand (see Review of supply, demand and inventories for September ). Strong Norwegian pipeline flows also supported the European storage injections in September. While maintenance outages were in line with our forecast and just 13% lower YoY, imports into continental Europe surged 26% YoY as the UK absorbed a disproportionate share of the disruption, with Norwegian flows to the UK almost halving. This pushed September Norwegian pipeline deliveries to continental Europe to their highest level in our dataset, surpassing the previous high recorded in 2022. This is not necessarily a bullish signal – historically, a reading near or below -2 has signalled a better opportunity to ‘buy the dip’, or at least to turn less bearish. However, our RAI principal components illustrate a regime shift – RAI PC1 (‘Global Growth’) has started to ‘catch down’ to RAI PC2 (‘Monetary Policy’) after decoupling for most of the year (Exhibit 7). For most of the year, the RAI has stayed at elevated levels supported by growth sentiment, but recently RAI PC1 has declined, with rate sensitive parts within equities such as small and mid caps suffering, with sharp increases in credit spreads and, more recently, Euro area sovereign spreads. For some economies, currencies can plausibly play an important role in rebalancing; for others, the required moves become so large that the more important conclusion is that adjustment will ultimately have to come through other channels and policy decisions that affect saving and investment. Our Fundamental Equilibrium Exchange Rate (FEER) model can help tackle this question. However, it requires looking at FEER from a different direction. Our existing FEER framework introduced last year (see Global FXEM Strategy: Assessing Fair Value in FX: A FEER Approach, 26th Sep, 2025) asks what level of the real effective exchange rate is consistent with an external position justified by the economy's broader fundamentals. The new exercise reverses the causal lens: if we change the exchange rate, how much does the external balance change, and what currency adjustment would be required to close the gap? It is deliberately an FX-only counterfactual. It is not another estimate of equilibrium fair value, nor should the resulting currency moves be interpreted as forecasts or trading targets.

records.text: Giving credit to balance — bonds gradually moving from headwind to hedge 1. Risky assets have consolidated since the start of the summer with rates and energy price headwinds taking over from earnings growth tailwinds in 2H. Upward pressure on global bond yields has picked up due to a combination of sticky inflation and resilient growth resulting in more hawkish central banks, but also fiscal concerns coupled with increasing capital competition due to the financing of the AI capex boom. Global equities in aggregate have been range-bound despite continued strong underlying earnings growth – as a result they de-rated materially alongside rising bond yields. Depending on the location and persistence of atmospheric blocking, it could also coincide with low-wind Dunkelflaute episodes, potentially lifting gas-for-power demand at the same time as heating consumption. These low wind, cold snaps can drive spikes in gas prices if occurring against a backdrop of low inventories in peak demand months Jan/Feb, as concerns around deliverability of supply from storage arise. In a truly cold winter scenario, while unlikely this winter, Europe still risks reaching record low inventory levels of only 5%. At that level, falling reservoir pressure would likely constrain withdrawal rates and severely strain system deliverability. Avoiding this outcome and ensuring a safer minimum fill level of ~15% would require LNG imports to rise by >15% YoY against a likely tight LNG market backdrop. ng series: timely, parsimonious, all-weather A key motivation for revising the input series was to make the indicator more forward- looking. The updated specification places greater emphasis on higher-frequency market data, reducing the impact of publication lags associated with some monthly releases. The revised framework also adopts a more streamlined approach to correlated signals. Highly related indicators are either consolidated into a single measure, such as combining 1-month and 3-month risk reversals or grouped in a way that prevents any single theme from dominating the aggregate signal. For example, CFTC positioning is now represented by three broader positioning measures that are averaged together. records.text: hat the stronger currency account is sustainable. A positive terms-of-trade shock, for example, can simultaneously raise export income, strengthen the external balance and support an appreciation in the REER. The same can be true of productivity improvements. But the observed macroeconomic relationship need not look like that: Indeed, an alternative perspective is, what if the exchange rate is in the driving seat and the sole driver of the external balance? What change in the exchange rate is required in order to force the external position of the economy into balance? Here the causality runs in the opposite direction. Viewed narrowly through the trade channel, a real appreciation makes exports less competitive and imports cheaper, weakening the trade and current-account balance over time. Under that one-way causal interpretation, a country running an excessive surplus should require currency appreciation to restore external balance, while an excessive deficit should require depreciation ( Exhibit 4 ). Investors often think about exchange rates from this perspective, particularly in Emerging Markets, as the exchange rate is sometimes viewed as a policy tool, with misalignments deliberately corrected through exchange rate adjustments as part of an overall macroeconomic adjustment programme to help restore a more sustainable external position.

records.text: M Global Foundation 18 Two implications follow for the import equation. First, an economy's import prices can shift materially while its trade-weighted rate barely moves, simply because the dollar moved, so the REER can miss price changes that importers actually face. Second, exchange-rate pass-through into any single economy's import prices is lower than a producer-currency model would predict, because dollar-invoiced prices are sticky in dollars and do not reprice with each bilateral move. Both make the trade-weighted rate a noisier measure of the price importers pay. We therefore additionally estimate each economy's import response to an invoicing-weighted exchange rate, to test whether it explains import volumes better than the REER. We use the USD and EUR import-invoicing shares from the Boz et al. (2022) dataset as fixed weights, since invoicing patterns change very slowly over time. The index combines the log of local currency per dollar and per euro, each weighted by its invoicing share and deflated by relative consumer prices, and is oriented to rise with an appreciation so it is directly comparable with the REER. For the euro area, the shares refer to extra-area imports. records.text: s assured, noting that sufficient gas remains available on the global market. Has the storage filling level become a less relevant indicator of security of supply? Indeed, the current gas storage level may have become a less important indicator of supply security than in the past. Germany and Europe now source a larger share of their gas from the global LNG market rather than via pipelines, potentially shortening the time lag between imports and consumption. The growing importance of spot markets may therefore have reduced the need for the traditional winter preparedness model based on high storage levels. In addition, industrial gas consumption in Europe has declined structurally since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, as many gas-intensive industrial facilities have exited the market. As a result, all else being equal, less gas needs to be held in storage for this customer group. The national gas reserve may contribute to that development in the medium term. Although it is intended to be used only in exceptional circumstances, over time it could help make markets less sensitive to low gas storage levels at the start of the winter season. This could, in turn, have a stabilising effect on gas prices. Overall, we maintain our view that the risk of a physical gas shortage in Germany is currently of less relevance. By contrast, the growth-dampening and inflationary effects of higher gas prices appear to be the more significant concern (see also our report form early September)

However, we think a pause in QT would not stop the term- premium decompression, only slow it marginally as reinvestment flows would not be able to overpower the natural ageing of overall portfolios. Furthermore, adjusting balance sheet policy to address financial conditions, even if done in a time-limited fashion, would be inconsistent with the ECB's monetary policy strategy statement that explicitly states that policy rates are their primary monetary policy instrument. In sum, we think any change to the ECB's balance sheet policy with regards to APP/PEPP QT as well as reinvestment flexibility would be akin to applying a ' duct tape to a leaking pipe' , and hence would be unlikely. That said, we discuss below the potential money market implications of a stop in the ECB's quantitative normalisation journey. This week: Favorable supply-demand conditions persist following early- month auctions This week saw a continuation of the favorable supply-demand conditions that followed last week’s opening of the auction cycle. The JGB market began the week with buying concentrated in the long end as the global rise in yields paused, resulting in a twist-flattening of the curve. The results of the 5y JGB auction on the 14th were somewhat soft but broadly benign and did not prompt a reversal in supply-demand sentiment. The USD itself sits toward the depreciation end of the bilateral ladder: Most currencies in the universe would need to adjust higher against it as part of global coordinated move toward external balance, even though the size of that adjustment varies substantially. The heatmap extends this comparison to every possible pair. We can read each cell as the adjustment of the row currency against the column currency: a positive number indicates upward adjustments for the row currency against the column currency, while a negative number indicates downward adjustments required. The largest pairwise gaps occur between currencies at opposite ends of the reconstructed ladder. PEN/PHP is the widest implied cross, followed by KRW/PHP and SEK/PHP. These pairs are not necessarily the most practical expressions of the signal given limited direct liquidity; rather, they illustrate the degree of dispersion embedded in the bilateral system. In practice, the more useful application would be to identify liquid crosses or USD legs that express the same relative-required adjustments. We estimate that bond funds have become underweight duration through the n selloff, reaching the sort of extreme that has on average seen lower yields over the subsequent 1-to-2 quarters. Negative convexity dynamics related to MBS and Treasury futures have likely amplified moves over the last month but should be a much smaller factor in further selloffs. A range of considerations have put US duration on better footing and argue for a n more bullish stance, in our view. Yields are elevated versus macro fundamentals, positioning is underweight, and technical risks have diminished. Energy remains an important source of day-to-day vol for global rates, but pressures in credit markets have started to set boundaries on selloffs. Diminished growth optimism or reduced energy risks would likely take yields n lower quickly. Under our fundamental view that underlying inflation pressures are contained amid limited evidence of overheating, front-end pricing is too hawkish and there is risk premium through the US curve. It may be a more gradual process, but an accumulation of news that supports that view can also support lower yields. The clearest route to a near-term peak in global yields would be tighter financial conditions weakening growth sentiment; recent pressure in corporate and sovereign credit suggests the sell-off may already be approaching a speed limit. The Euro area sovereign risk concerns also generated a relative safety bid, with US, German and UK 10-year bonds rallying as OAT spreads widened. We remain overweight the US, UK and Germany, and underweight Japan for 12m (UK N for 3m). We shift UW credit for 3m and remain UW for 12m. Credit has underperformed equities in the recent ‘risk off’ environment, extending the underperformance YTD. After the recent widening owing to elevated rates volatility and continued concerns on supply, credit spreads are close to our credit strategy team’s year-end targets. They see potential for some typical year-end spread tightening, which is often visible in late December, as the pace of supply slows. However, they see risks to their forecasts as tilted towards more widening. While all-in yields are higher, credit spreads remain relatively low – for example for the USD IG corporate index, the credit spread accounts for only 15% of the yield (compared with 45% on average in recent years).
